articles.title: Make your mobile app findable by AI search
articles.description: If you ship a mobile app, how do AI search tools find it and describe it correctly? They read your website and your store listing, not your app binary. An app with a thin site and a one-line listing gets summarized from whatever scraps exist, and that is how wrong prices and made-up features end up in an answer box. This post covers what a founder who ships a mobile app can fix in an afternoon: the site the app points to, the structured data on it, the store listing, the link between the two, and what the coding agent in your editor reads once it opens your project. It is the mobile half of a topic that web-app guides cover well, such as the Open SaaS guide. That guide's advice (prerender your marketing pages, add JSON-LD, publish an llms.txt file, set meta and Open Graph tags) applies to a mobile app's website too. It stops at the website. A mobile app has more surfaces than that. Surface one: the website, readable without JavaScript The first step is the same for any product. The page a crawler or an assistant fetches has to contain the real content in its HTML. If your marketing site renders everything on the client, an assistant that does not run a full browser sees an empty shell and fills the gap from other sources. We wrote up the failure and the fix in Your website has two front doors, including the check: run curl on your home page and read what comes back. Do that check on three pages: the home page, the page that describes the app, and the pricing or download page. If a price, a platform list or a feature only appears in the browser after scripts run, it does not exist for a reader that skips scripts. Surface two: structured data that says "mobile app" Meta tags tell a crawler about a page. Structured data tells it what the page is. For a mobile app the useful type is MobileApplication, which Schema.org defines as a software application designed to work well on a mobile device. It sits under SoftwareApplication, so every property of that parent is available. A minimal block for your app's page, inside a script tag of type application/ld+json, looks like this: Two properties do most of the work: operatingSystem says where it runs and applicationCategory says what kind of app it is. Once your app is live, add downloadUrl and set it to the address of your real store listing, so the block points at the binary. Pair it with Organization and WebSite blocks on the home page, and an FAQPage block on a page that answers real questions. Validate before you deploy with Google's Rich Results Test or the Schema.org validator. One honest limit: structured data raises the odds that a crawler reads your facts correctly. It does not guarantee a citation, and we have no measured data that it moves the number of installs. Surface three: the store listing Assistants that answer "best app for X" questions often cite the store page, because it is a page with ratings, a category and a description that you do not control the layout of. Treat the listing text as something a machine will read: Say what the app does in the first sentence of the description. Not a slogan: who it is for and what they do with it. Use the same name, price and platform list as your site. A listing that says free and a site that says paid gives an assistant two answers, and it will pick one. Write the subtitle and short description as plain claims you can defend. If the app does not send push notifications today, do not imply it. Keep one source of truth, a short markdown file in your repo with the name, one-line description, platforms, price and category. Paste from it into the listing, the MobileApplication block and the site. When a fact changes, change it once. Surface four: the link between site and app Search and assistants treat the app and the site as one product more readily if you tie them together. Both platforms have a standard way to prove that a domain belongs to an app. On Android, the system fetches a Digital Asset Links file named assetlinks.json from the /.well-known/ folder of each host in your app's intent filters, as Android's App Links documentation (read 22 Nov 2026) describes. On Android 15 and later the system re-verifies in the background, so a change to that file can take up to seven days to reach every device. On iOS the equivalent is an apple-app-site-association file on the same domain plus an associated-domains entry in the app (Apple documents this; we did not re-read the page for this post). The same link helps a person: a link shared from your site opens the app when it is installed and the site when it is not. Check it on a real device, not in the browser. The adb shell pm get-app-links command in the Android documentation prints a verification state for each domain, and verified is the one you want. Surface five: what the coding agent reads Discoverability has a second reader that founders forget: the coding agent that will edit your app. Claude Code, Cursor and similar tools read project files at the root before they write anything. A CLAUDE.md file holds instructions for Claude Code, .cursorrules holds Cursor's rules, and AGENTS.md is a plain file several other tools read. If those files are missing, the agent guesses your stack and your conventions on every prompt. This is what we ship in our own kits. Per our for-agents page and the kit folders on internal main (commit 8ab782e, read 22 Nov 2026), the Booking Kit, the AI SaaS Kit and the Marketplace Kit each carry CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and .cursorrules at the kit root, plus a folder of task prompts: 20 for the Booking Kit, 26 for the AI SaaS Kit and 21 for the Marketplace Kit. The prompt files are named for the change you will ask for, such as adding time zones or deposits to bookings. The files are written for the agent, not for a reader, and they are the same contract a new engineer would want on day one. There is a separate, site-level layer too. Our website serves an llms.txt index of every page, generated from the same inventory as the sitemap so the two cannot drift, and a markdown copy of most pages under /md/. That is for assistants reading the website. The kit files are for the agent inside your editor. They are different files for different readers, and a mobile app needs both. An afternoon checklist Run curl on your home, app and pricing pages. Fix anything that needs scripts to show a price or a platform. Add a MobileApplication block to the app page, and Organization plus WebSite to the home page. Write the one-source-of-truth facts file. Rewrite the store listing's first sentence from it. Host the Android Digital Asset Links file and the iOS association file, then test the Android result with adb shell pm get-app-links. Add CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md to your repo: stack with versions, one rule per concern, and a list of what is out of scope. Publish an llms.txt at your site root. Keep it short and hand-picked, not a copy of the sitemap, unless you generate it from the same inventory. What we do not know We have not measured whether any of these steps changes how often an assistant recommends an app. The keyword behind this topic was below what OpenSEO could measure on 11 Nov 2026, so search demand is small, and the value today is correctness: when an assistant does describe your app, the facts it reads are yours. The effort is an afternoon, and every step is reversible. If your next app is a booking or scheduling product, you can start from one that already has the agent files and the Supabase, Stripe and slot logic in place. The Booking Kit is an Expo app with a typed API server for checkout and reminders, a database rule that blocks double bookings, and a CLAUDE.md, an AGENTS.md and 20 task prompts for your agent: https://otf-kit.dev/templates/booking-kit. It is $99 one-time with 12 months of updates, and the demo is linked from the page. Sources Open SaaS, "SEO and AI discoverability for your SaaS" (prerendering, JSON-LD types, llms.txt, meta and Open Graph), https://docs.opensaas.sh/blog/2026-05-29-seo-and-ai-discoverability-for-your-saas/, dated 29 May 2026, read 22 Nov 2026. Schema.org, MobileApplication type (definition, parent SoftwareApplication, operatingSystem, applicationCategory, downloadUrl), https://schema.org/MobileApplication, read 22 Nov 2026. Android Developers, "Verify Android App Links" (assetlinks.json path, adb pm get-app-links, re-verification latency), https://developer.android.com/training/app-links/verify-android-applinks, read 22 Nov 2026. llms.txt proposal, https://llmstxt.org/, version 2, last modified 10 Aug 2026, read 22 Nov 2026. OTF, "Your website has two front doors. Your AI agent uses the worse one.", https://otf-kit.dev/blog/make-your-website-agent-readable, dated 7 Jul 2026, read 22 Nov 2026. OTF for-agents page and llms.txt route source (kit agent files, prompt counts, site index), otf-kit/internal main commit 8ab782e, read 22 Nov 2026. OTF Booking Kit page, https://otf-kit.dev/templates/booking-kit, read 22 Nov 2026 ($99 one-time, 12 months of updates, Expo SDK 58, Supabase, Stripe checkout).

articles.title: Auditing OpenAI Codex Desktop: 516-Token Cutoffs, Live 1 MiB Git Diffs, and Unzeroed SQLite
articles.description: Co-authored equally by Denis Vaulin (GitHub · LinkedIn) and Oleksii Mai (GitHub · LinkedIn). Interactive Forensic Report: nehumorist.github.io/codex-local-audit Offline Read-Only MIT Auditor (Node.js & Python): github.com/NeHumorist/codex-local-audit In October 2026, OpenAI Codex Desktop running in high / ultra reasoning mode started dropping reasoning output and hiding reasoning summaries while burning through subscription quota faster. Rather than guess from UI symptoms, we ran a cross-platform forensic audit across: 1,502 local ~/.codex/ session rollouts across Windows 11 x64 (215 sessions / 34,523 calls) and macOS arm64 (1,287 sessions / 160,172 calls), plus an independent third-party Pro reproduction across 246.8k calls; Signed client binaries (OpenAI.Codex_26.1111.2228.0 on Windows x64 and v26.1111.71704 on macOS arm64 — both codex and app.asar) cross-checked against the public openai/codex Rust repository; Local SQLite stores (queue_1.sqlite, logs_2.sqlite, thread_history_1.sqlite, codex-dev.db, memories_1.sqlite) and dictation-history/; Two official EU GDPR "Export Data" archives from OpenAI. Everything below is reproducible offline on your own machine in 5 seconds using our read-only MIT tool. 1. The Quantized 516-Token Cutoff Wall (518k - 2 Harmonics) Across both our Plus/Pro datasets and an independent third-party Pro user's 246.8k-call dataset, reasoning output exhibits a sharp discontinuity at exactly 516 tokens: Dataset Calls at 515 Calls at 516 Calls at 517 1034 (2 blocks) 1552 (3 blocks) 2070 (4 blocks) 3rd-Party Pro (246.8k calls) 70 9,021 0 1,280 384 139 macOS (160.2k calls) — 9,392 1 1,608 497 169 Three checks confirm this is not a tokenizer quirk or a simple rate-limit artifact: Harmonic spacing at 518k - 2: spikes repeat cleanly at 516, 1034, 1552, and 2070 reasoning tokens. Ciphertext byte-length correlation (r = 0.99538): reasoning_output_tokens tracks the raw encrypted_content ciphertext byte lengths directly (rTok == 0 calls carry 0 encrypted reasoning bytes). Not a quota ceiling: 71.2% (and 78.7% on macOS) of exact-516 cutoffs occurred below 80% on both the 5-hour and 7-day subscription windows. Alongside this cutoff, turn_context.summary silently flipped from "detailed" to "none" without a client update. 2. Live 1 MiB Raw git diff Capture Firing While Opted Out Inspecting signed app.asar (907538.0572f09d40.js, verified byte-for-byte across Windows and macOS builds) shows a telemetry payload (codex_turn_diff_event) that captures up to 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes) of raw unified git diff source code (diff, between_turn_diff, session_start_diff, visualization_diff, repository_full_name, commit/tree SHAs) and sends it to /wham/analytics-events/events. The gate checks only is_zdr === false and Statsig gate 586515394 — performing zero checks of training_allowed: false or [analytics] enabled = false. In live Windows Desktop runtime logs (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Codex\Logs, 2026-11-05), we captured post-gate execution (method=turn-diff-capture-complete workerId=git -> Failed to complete turn diff analytics capture) tied to the exact EU account whose official OpenAI GDPR export records: 3. Windows Explorer UserAssist Scraping & Default-On Analytics Inside signed app.asar, embedded PowerShell (Get-UserAssistEntries, Decode-Rot13) reads Windows Explorer's HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\UserAssist\*\Count registry keys and writes a catalog of installed third-party applications (last_used, use_count) to ~/.codex/cache/computer-use/computer-use-app-catalog/.../user-assist.json. On our Windows test host, user-assist.json cached 82 non-OpenAI applications (alongside 28 [external-agent-import] scans of competitor directories like ~/.claude and .cursor). At the same time, while OpenAI's Rust CLI source (cli/src/main.rs) comments that analytics default to off for app-server, Electron unconditionally passes --analytics-default-enabled, and Codex Settings provides 0 UI toggles to disable telemetry. 4. Local SQLite Erasure Gaps, Microphone Retention & Incomplete GDPR Exports 0 calls to PRAGMA secure_delete across all 10,502 files of openai/codex and signed binaries: queue_1.sqlite measured 98.6% unzeroed freelist pages at 0 live rows (+ recoverable prompts in -wal), and logs_2.sqlite measured 90.6%–91.8% unzeroed deleted pages. thread_history_1.sqlite contains 0 ON DELETE CASCADE foreign keys and is skipped by StateRuntime::delete_thread. dictation-history/ retains unencrypted local Opus microphone audio + transcripts with zero TTL (54+ days on Windows; up to 78 days including cancelled captures on macOS). Plaintext auth.json on Windows: codex_desktop_secret_auth_storage explicitly excludes Windows. 0 of 1,502 Codex sessions appeared across two official EU GDPR "Export Data" archives (150.8 MB and 186.8 MB), even though export_manifest.json reported "omissions": []. 5. Negative Controls: What We Checked and Ruled Out To keep every claim anchored strictly to verifiable bytes, our report explicitly documents 10 hypotheses we checked and ruled out, including: CodexWindowsSystemSerialObserved (gate 1259783540): unhashed Windows BIOS serial collection and local debug-log redaction are compiled into signed app.asar, but the gate had not activated on our test host. 0 local model_reroute events inside ~/.codex/sessions/ JSONL records. Standard 5h/7d quota exhaustion (ruled out because >71% of 516 cutoffs occurred below 80% quota). Verify Your Own Machine in 5 Seconds (MIT, Read-Only, Offline) codex-local-audit has full feature parity across zero-dependency Node.js (22.15+ / 24+) and Python 3.10+. It opens every SQLite database strictly read-only, makes zero network calls, never opens or reads auth.json, and strips all prompts, code, app names, and file paths. git clone https://github.com/NeHumorist/codex-local-audit.git cd codex-local-audit # Node.js 22.15+ / 24+ (zero external dependencies) node audit_codex.mjs # Or Python 3.10–3.13 via uv uv run --with zstandard python audit_codex.py On Windows without a global Node 24 install, you can invoke the Node 24 runtime already bundled with Codex Desktop: $node24 = Get-ChildItem "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\*\bin\node.exe" | Select-Object -First 1 -ExpandProperty FullName & $node24 .\audit_codex.mjs Interactive Forensic Report: https://nehumorist.github.io/codex-local-audit/ Source Code (MIT): https://github.com/NeHumorist/codex-local-audit If you run the audit on Codex Plus or Pro, feel free to share anonymized counts in the comments — we are especially interested in whether the 516 / 1034 / 1552 pattern reproduces on newer builds.

I built an AI deal bot on a Mac mini — but a human approves every post
articles.description: Why I built it I'm an IT director by day in Raleigh, NC. I love a good deal, but I hate deal sites. Most of them post everything: 70%-off off-brand gadgets, "deals" on laptops with 8 GB of RAM, sales that ended three hours ago. You scroll past 50 bad items to find one good one. So I built Snag Bag Deals (snagbagdeals.com): a small deal site where software does the scanning and a person does the deciding. A Python bot on a Mac mini in my house reads deal feeds all day, an AI model throws out the junk, and every survivor lands on my phone as a card I approve or skip. Nothing goes public without a tap from me. It's been live about a week. In that time the bot has looked at more than 16,000 items, sent me about 1,150 approval cards, and I've posted 278 deals. Here's how it works, what it costs, and what went wrong. How it works The pipeline has four steps, and only the last one is me. Deal feeds. The bot polls 13 RSS feeds and deal pages (Slickdeals, DealNews, 9to5Toys, camelcamelcamel and others) every few minutes and pulls out the store link. Keyword rules. Cheap checks run first, before any AI call: a blocklist, duplicates, stores I don't support, and "save up to X%" sale pages that aren't one product. AI filter. Whatever survives goes to Claude's smallest model with my written guidelines ("good items people will get use out of, not something they regret"). It answers keep or skip, picks a category, cleans up the title and writes a one-line blurb. My recent taps are included as examples, so it learns my taste. My approval. Keepers arrive in Telegram as a card with the price, the source and Post / Skip / Never buttons. One tap publishes to the static site (rebuilt and deployed to Cloudflare Pages within a minute), a Telegram channel, and an email roundup twice a week. Facebook and Threads only get the few best deals each day, spread out, so the feeds don't read like spam. Keeping deals honest after they post A deal is only good while the price holds, and Amazon prices move hourly. Without access to Amazon's product API (it unlocks after 10 sales in 30 days), the bot can't read live prices, and scraping Amazon is against the affiliate rules. So it leans on a few cheaper signals: Source checks. It re-opens each deal's original post and looks for "expired" or "sold out" in the title. Slickdeals and friends mark dead deals quickly. Flash deals expire on a timer. Lightning deals and today-only deals are marked dead when their window closes, no check needed. A morning check, riskiest first. Each morning I get up to 10 deals to eyeball, ranked by how likely they are to be wrong: promo-code deals, Lightning deals, anything over 60% off. One tap marks a dead one. Visitor reports. Every card has an "Expired? Report it" button. Fix once, fix everywhere. One command corrects a price on the site, the Telegram post, the live Facebook post and any social posts still in the queue. Expired deals get edited to say so on each platform that allows edits. The site also stops showing a price once a deal is a day old and labels it "check price," which is more honest than a stale number. What it costs to run The whole thing runs for about the price of the domain. The AI filter is the only metered cost, and it's small because it uses a fast, cheap model on short prompts. Piece What runs it Cost The bot Python on a Mac mini I already own (also my Plex server) $0 AI filtering and blurbs Claude's smallest model via API about 14 cents a day Website + hosting Static pages on Cloudflare Pages Analytics A Cloudflare Pages Function writing to Analytics Engine Email roundup Kit, free plan Domain Cloudflare Registrar about $11 a year The bot is light enough to share a home server: about 50 MB of memory and a couple percent of one CPU core on average. It logs its own costs too. Every API charge, receipt and payout lands in a small money log, which feeds a private stats page and a CSV for taxes. Analytics are first-party and cookie-free. The page sends a tiny beacon to my own endpoint with the page, the source and whether it was a click out. No IP addresses are stored, no profiles, no Google Analytics. What went wrong (so far) The bot read a store credit as the price. A headset deal mentioned a gift-card bonus, and the parser took that dollar amount as the sale price. Now amounts next to words like "credit," "gift card" and "rebate" are ignored. "eCoupon at checkout" slipped past it. A $47 meat thermometer posted at $14.99 because the deal needed a one-time promo code the bot didn't recognize. It catches that wording now, and promo-code deals get flagged for a check the next morning. "Clip the coupon" was too broad. Some deals need a coupon you tick on the page; others apply a discount at checkout. Calling both "clip the coupon" sent people looking for a box that wasn't there, so they're two different labels now. Posting fast from a new account looks like spam. Bluesky flagged the account after a burst of link posts on day one. Now social accounts get only the few best deals a day, spaced out. The site and Telegram still get everything. Affiliate networks want traffic first. Two networks turned the site down this week, politely, for being too new. Amazon's product API also waits until you have sales. The fix is boring: keep posting good deals and grow. What's next The building part went fast. I wrote it with Claude as a pair programmer, and the first working version took about a week of evenings. The hard part now is the one AI doesn't do for you: getting people to show up and trust it. Next up is a reader request form that already exists but needs readers: tell me what you're shopping for, a daily job hunts for it, and matches get a Reader request tag. After that, product photos once Amazon's API opens up. I'd love feedback, especially on two things: Would you use a curated deal site like this, or are deals strictly a "go to Slickdeals" thing for you? If you've grown a small content site from zero, what channel actually worked: email, Telegram, search, something else? The site is snagbagdeals.com. Happy to answer questions about the bot in the comments. Disclosure: Snag Bag Deals earns a commission from Amazon and other stores on qualifying purchases, at no extra cost to you.

articles.title: Graph Neural Networks: How They Work and Their Uses?
articles.description: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are changing how artificial intelligence understands complex relationships between connected data points. Unlike traditional machine learning models that process information as rows, tables, or independent data points, Graph Neural Networks analyze connections between entities and use those relationships to make predictions. This capability makes GNNs especially useful in areas where relationships carry as much meaning as the individual data itself. Examples include social networks, financial transactions, recommendation systems, drug discovery, and traffic prediction. As connected data becomes more important across industries, Graph Neural Networks are emerging as a powerful approach within modern machine learning. What Are Graph Neural Networks? A Graph Neural Network is a type of neural network designed to process graph-structured data. A graph consists of two main elements: • Nodes: Represent individual entities, such as people, products, websites, or chemical compounds. • Edges: Represent relationships or connections between those entities. For example, in a social network, each user can be represented as a node, while friendships or interactions between users are represented as edges. Traditional machine learning models may analyze individual user profiles, but a GNN can also examine how users are connected. This additional relationship information helps the model identify patterns that may not be visible when data points are analyzed independently. To understand the foundations, explore what a neural network is and how neural networks process information. How Does Graph Neural Network Architecture Work? The effectiveness of a GNN depends on how it represents graph data and learns from relationships. Its architecture generally includes nodes, edges, feature representations, and message-passing layers. A typical GNN follows three major steps: 1. Representing Data as a Graph First, the system converts available information into a graph structure. Each node receives features that describe its characteristics, while edges define how nodes are connected. For example, an e-commerce platform can represent customers and products as nodes. A purchase, review, or product interaction can become an edge connecting them. 2. Message Passing Between Nodes Message passing is one of the most important mechanisms in GNN architecture. During this process, each node collects information from its neighboring nodes. The model combines this information with the node's existing features to create an updated representation. For instance, a customer node may receive information from connected products and other interaction patterns. This helps the model understand more than the customer's individual purchase history. 3. Updating Node Representations After collecting information from neighboring nodes, the GNN updates each node's representation using an aggregation function and a neural network. This process can repeat across multiple layers. With each layer, a node can learn from a wider neighborhood within the graph. The final representations can then support tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. How Message Passing Helps GNNs Understand Relationships? Message passing allows Graph Neural Networks to learn from connected information instead of treating every data point separately. For example, imagine a financial network containing thousands of bank accounts and transactions. A traditional model may examine transaction amounts, locations, and account activity. A GNN can also analyze how accounts are connected through transaction relationships. This makes it possible to identify unusual connection patterns that could indicate coordinated fraudulent activity. The model does not simply look at one transaction. It learns from the surrounding network structure, which can provide valuable context for more accurate predictions. Major Types of Graph Neural Networks Different GNN architectures are designed to handle different graph structures and learning requirements. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) Graph Convolutional Networks learn by combining information from neighboring nodes. They are commonly used for node classification and semi-supervised learning tasks. Graph Attention Networks (GATs) Graph Attention Networks use attention mechanisms to assign different importance levels to neighboring nodes. This allows the model to focus more strongly on relationships that provide useful information. GraphSAGE GraphSAGE generates node representations by sampling and aggregating information from neighboring nodes. It is useful for large graphs where processing every connection may be computationally expensive. Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs) GINs are designed to improve the ability of graph neural networks to distinguish different graph structures. They are useful in graph classification and research involving molecular structures. Real-World Applications of Graph Neural Networks Graph Neural Networks are valuable wherever connected data can reveal patterns that traditional approaches may overlook. 1. Fraud Detection in Financial Networks Financial institutions can use GNNs to analyze relationships between accounts, transactions, devices, and payment activities. Instead of examining suspicious transactions individually, these models can identify unusual network patterns, helping financial teams investigate potentially coordinated fraud. 2. Recommendation Systems Recommendation platforms can represent users, products, and interactions as connected nodes. By learning from these relationships, GNNs can identify products that may interest a customer based on similar users, previous interactions, and product connections. 3. Drug Discovery and Healthcare Research Molecules can be represented as graphs, where atoms are nodes and chemical bonds are edges. GNNs can analyze molecular structures to support predictions about chemical properties, molecular interactions, and potential drug candidates. These predictions can assist research, although experimental validation remains essential. 4. Social Network Analysis Social platforms contain large networks of users and their interactions. GNNs can help identify communities, predict relationships, and analyze how information spreads through connected networks. 5. Traffic Prediction and Transportation Road networks can be represented as graphs, with intersections as nodes and roads as edges. GNNs can analyze traffic conditions across connected locations to support traffic forecasting, route planning, and transportation management. Graph Neural Networks vs. Traditional Machine Learning Traditional machine learning models generally work with structured features and often treat each record as an independent example. Graph Neural Networks are different because they explicitly use relationships between entities during learning. For example, a traditional fraud detection model may examine transaction amount, time, and location. A GNN can also analyze the relationships between accounts involved in those transactions. Both approaches have value. The best choice depends on the structure of the data and the problem being solved. For a broader understanding of these technologies, read machine learning fundamentals and the differences between AI, machine learning, and deep learning. Challenges and Limitations of Graph Neural Networks Despite their capabilities, GNNs also introduce technical challenges that developers and researchers need to consider. • Computational complexity: Large graphs with millions of nodes and edges can require significant processing resources. • Data quality: Missing, incorrect, or incomplete relationships can affect model performance. • Oversmoothing: When too many message-passing layers are applied, node representations may become increasingly similar. • Scalability: Processing very large and continuously changing graphs requires efficient sampling and optimization techniques. • Interpretability: Understanding why a GNN makes a particular prediction can be difficult, especially in high-stakes applications. Addressing these challenges requires careful architecture selection, data preparation, testing, and model evaluation. The Future of Graph Neural Networks Graph Neural Networks are becoming increasingly relevant as organizations work with complex and interconnected datasets. Research is expanding their use in areas such as knowledge graphs, scientific discovery, cybersecurity, autonomous systems, and large-scale recommendation platforms. They are also being combined with other AI techniques, including transformers and large language models, to improve how systems reason over connected information. As graph-based data becomes more widely available, GNNs are likely to remain an important part of advanced machine learning research and practical AI development. Developers and technology enthusiasts can also explore the DEV Community to discover technical tutorials, share knowledge, and stay informed about emerging developments in AI and machine learning. Conclusion Graph Neural Networks provide a powerful way to understand information that is naturally connected. By learning from both individual entities and their relationships, they can solve problems that may be difficult for traditional machine learning approaches. From financial fraud detection to drug discovery and recommendation systems, GNNs are creating new opportunities for analyzing complex data. Their continued development will make them increasingly important in the future of artificial intelligence and graph-based machine learning. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) 1. What are Graph Neural Networks used for? Graph Neural Networks are used for tasks involving connected data, including fraud detection, recommendation systems, drug discovery, social network analysis, and traffic prediction. 2. How are GNNs different from traditional neural networks? Traditional neural networks generally process structured inputs such as images, text, or numerical features. GNNs are specifically designed to process graph data and learn from relationships between connected nodes. 3. What is message passing in GNNs? Message passing is the process through which a node collects information from its neighboring nodes, combines that information, and updates its representation. 4. What are the main types of Graph Neural Networks? Common architectures include Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), Graph Attention Networks (GATs), GraphSAGE, and Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs). 5. Are Graph Neural Networks part of deep learning? Yes. Graph Neural Networks are a category of deep learning models designed to learn from graph-structured data and relationships between entities.

articles.title: Windows Restarted Our Counter PCs at Ten to Seven Because Their Active Hours Were Set for Head Office
articles.description: Our branch counters open at half past six. The first hour is the busiest of the day, because builders collect what they need before they drive to site. Counter staff switch their PCs on when they arrive and off when they lock up, as we asked them to years ago to save electricity. At ten to seven one Thursday in February 2025, the PCs on the counters at twenty six branches put up a message saying they would restart shortly, then restarted and spent up to fifteen minutes installing an update. Builders queued. Some counters wrote orders on paper and keyed them in later. Head office noticed nothing, because nobody there was at a desk before eight. Windows lets us set active hours, the part of the day when it will not restart a PC to finish installing updates. We set them for every PC by policy, from eight in the morning to six in the evening, which describes head office very well. We also set a deadline: once an update has waited a few days, Windows stops asking and restarts at the next moment outside active hours. For a PC that is switched on at half past six and off at half past five, that moment comes once a day, at the start of trading. Every month most counter PCs had postponed the restart until the deadline passed, and every month it fell due on a morning. That Thursday it fell due on most of them at once. Nothing was misconfigured in the sense of an error. One policy described one working day, and we applied it to a business that keeps several. Counter, warehouse and transport office PCs are now in their own groups, each with active hours that match its real day. Counter PCs are protected from six in the morning until midnight, and they are no longer switched off at closing. Instead they go to sleep, and our device management wakes them at two in the morning on the second night after each monthly update, installs it and restarts them while the branch is locked. A report each morning lists every counter PC with a restart still pending, and the service desk rings the branch the day before a deadline rather than the morning after. Out of hours is not a single time of day. Before you let software choose when to interrupt people, ask each part of the business when its working day actually begins. – Serguey Shinder

articles.title: vLLM production metrics: running an OpenAI-compatible server with Prometheus and GPU monitoring
articles.description: Putting vLLM into production means moving from an LLM that « works on my machine » to an inference service able to absorb hundreds of concurrent requests on datacentre GPUs. Born in a lab at the University of California, Berkeley and now hosted by the PyTorch Foundation, vLLM is one of the most followed open source projects on GitHub for serving language models. This guide covers the vLLM production metrics that matter, alongside the OpenAI-compatible server and GPU monitoring. Its strength rests on two ideas: PagedAttention, which manages the key-value cache (KV cache) memory in pages, the way an operating system manages virtual memory, and continuous batching, which inserts new requests into the running batch instead of waiting for it to finish. The result: much better utilisation of GPUs, which are expensive. For an SRE, vLLM has another quality: it natively exposes a rich Prometheus endpoint and can emit OpenTelemetry traces. Let us see how to install it, run it as an OpenAI-compatible server, then monitor it all the way into Dynatrace. Why choose vLLM in production? vLLM meets a specific need: serving open models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma…) from Hugging Face with high throughput. It offers: an HTTP server compatible with the OpenAI API (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/models…), so it can be used with existing SDKs; tensor and pipeline parallelism to spread a large model across several GPUs; support for many quantised formats and several hardware families (NVIDIA first and foremost, but also AMD and other accelerators depending on the version). Its limits: it assumes a serious GPU, its startup time is long (loading weights, compilation, memory pre-allocation) and its many settings require some experience. For a developer workstation, Ollama locally or llama.cpp are lighter. In practice: deploying an OpenAI-compatible vLLM server Step 1 — Install vLLM On a Linux machine with an NVIDIA GPU and recent CUDA drivers, installation is done with pip, preferably in a virtual environment: python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install vllm The supported combinations of Python, CUDA and PyTorch versions change often: check them in the official vLLM installation guide. Step 2 — Start the server The vllm serve command starts the OpenAI-compatible server, on port 8000 by default. For a gated model on Hugging Face, first export a token in HF_TOKEN: vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \ --max-model-len 8192 \ --api-key "$VLLM_API_KEY" --gpu-memory-utilization sets the fraction of GPU memory vLLM allows itself, --max-model-len limits the context length (and therefore the KV cache size), and --tensor-parallel-size spreads the model across several GPUs. The full list of options is available with vllm serve --help. Step 3 — Or use the Docker image docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \ -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -e HF_TOKEN="$HF_TOKEN" \ vllm/vllm-openai:latest \ --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct In production, replace latest with a specific version. On Kubernetes, the documentation offers deployment examples and community charts; allow a generous startup probe, as loading a large model takes several minutes. Step 4 — Test the API curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $VLLM_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]}' curl -s http://localhost:8000/health Which vLLM production metrics should you monitor in Prometheus? The server publishes its metrics in Prometheus format on /metrics, prefixed with vllm:. The exact names changed with the move to the « V1 » engine: check them by querying your own instance (curl localhost:8000/metrics) and the « Metrics » page of the documentation. The families to track: Load: running and waiting requests (vllm:num_requests_running, vllm:num_requests_waiting). A growing queue is the first sign of saturation. Memory: KV cache usage. Close to 100%, vLLM preempts requests and latency soars. Latency: histograms of time to first token (TTFT), inter-token time and end-to-end latency. Volume: counters of prompt tokens and generated tokens, the basis for throughput and cost calculations. Request outcome: number of requests finished by finish reason (maximum length, normal stop, abort). These application metrics are read alongside GPU metrics: utilisation, memory, power and temperature, provided by NVIDIA’s DCGM exporter (deployed by the GPU Operator on Kubernetes) or by a host agent. Logs and OpenTelemetry traces vLLM logs to standard output the model loading, the memory allocated to the KV cache and, periodically, a summary of throughput and cache usage. On Kubernetes, these logs are collected like those of any other pod. For traces, the server accepts an --otlp-traces-endpoint option that sends one span per request to an OTLP collector, with attributes inspired by the GenAI semantic conventions (model, tokens, time in queue, TTFT). The required OpenTelemetry packages must be installed separately; the documentation provides a complete example. If the calling application propagates W3C context, the vLLM span attaches to the end-to-end trace. Sending vLLM data to Dynatrace The simplest route is an OpenTelemetry Collector that scrapes /metrics, receives OTLP traces and exports everything. Dynatrace expects OTLP metrics with delta temporality: the cumulativetodelta processor converts cumulative Prometheus counters. receivers: prometheus: config: scrape_configs: - job_name: vllm scrape_interval: 15s static_configs: - targets: ["vllm:8000"] otlp: protocols: grpc: http: processors: cumulativetodelta: batch: exporters: otlphttp: endpoint: https://.live.dynatrace.com/api/v2/otlp headers: Authorization: "Api-Token ${env:DT_API_TOKEN}" service: pipelines: metrics: receivers: [prometheus] processors: [cumulativetodelta, batch] exporters: [otlphttp] traces: receivers: [otlp] processors: [batch] The token must carry metrics and traces ingest permissions. On Kubernetes, Dynatrace can also scrape annotated Prometheus endpoints directly; check its documentation to choose between the two approaches. Once the data is in Grail, a few dashboards are enough: p95 TTFT, waiting requests, KV cache usage, tokens per second and GPU utilisation per node. The principles of histogram-based SLOs, detailed in our article on histogram metrics with OpenPipeline, apply directly to TTFT. Best practices Pin the vLLM version and the model identifier; test every upgrade, as options and metrics change. Protect the API with a key and network filtering; do not expose it directly on the internet. Alert on the queue and KV cache usage before latency: they are leading indicators. Size --max-model-len according to real usage rather than the model’s maximum capacity. Keep prompts out of traces if they contain sensitive data. Frequently asked questions Is vLLM really compatible with the OpenAI API? For the main endpoints (chat, completions, models, embeddings depending on the model), yes: you just change the SDK’s base URL. Some advanced parameters may differ; the documentation lists those that are supported. Where can you find vLLM’s Prometheus metrics? On the server’s /metrics path, on the same port as the API. Names start with vllm:. Does vLLM work without a GPU? A CPU mode exists for some platforms, but vLLM is designed for accelerators. Without a GPU, llama.cpp or Ollama are better suited. Conclusion vLLM provides the throughput needed to serve open LLMs at scale, and it has the good sense to be observable straight after installation. By bringing its Prometheus metrics, its OTLP traces and GPU metrics together in a single backend, you can run inference like any other critical service. To choose between vLLM and the other building blocks, see our comparison of self-hosted open source AI stacks. span.observer is an independent community blog, not affiliated with Dynatrace LLC or the projects mentioned. articles.title: We moved our kiosk installer build into one cmd step and nothing after npm ever ran
articles.description: Our depot kiosks run a small Electron application, and its Windows installer used to be built by Jenkins on a Windows agent. The job had three bat steps: npm run dist, then signtool sign with our code signing certificate and a timestamp, then signtool verify /pa on the result. In September we moved it to GitHub Actions on a Windows runner. To keep the commands exactly as they were, we put all three lines into one step with shell: cmd. The workflow was green, the installer was uploaded to the release, and we moved on. Five weeks later a depot manager setting up a new kiosk sent us a screenshot of a blue box: Windows protected your PC, publisher unknown. Every installer we had published since the move was unsigned. npm on Windows is not a program. It is npm.cmd, a batch file. In a batch script, running another batch file by name hands control to it, and when it finishes, control does not come back to the line after it. The script simply ends there, with the exit code of the batch file it handed over to. You need call npm run dist to return. Jenkins had hidden this from us for years, because each bat step was its own script with one line in it. Our new step ran npm run dist, which succeeded, and stopped. The signing line never ran. Neither did the line that was there to verify the signing, which is the part that stung. The fix for that night was the word call. The fix we kept was structural. Each command now has its own step, so each has its own exit status, and the steps use the default pwsh shell instead of cmd. Verification is a separate step that runs Get-AuthenticodeSignature on every file we are about to publish and fails unless the status is Valid and the signer is our certificate. The release job only uploads what that step has checked. A short lint runs on every workflow change and fails any cmd step with more than one line. We re-signed and republished the three installers, and asked the depots to reinstall them. The script did not fail. It ended early, politely, and reported the success of the last thing it had done. – Sergey Shinder

articles.title: Actively exploited this week: 9 new CISA KEV entries (16 November to 22 November 2026)
articles.description: Every week CISA adds vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue. The bar for getting on that list is not "severe on paper" but "attackers are using it now". For a small team with limited patching hours, that makes KEV the most useful priority list there is. Below: every entry added between 16 November and 22 November 2026, copied from the catalogue and linked to its NVD record, plus what Romania's national cyber security directorate and Have I Been Pwned published in the same days. Nothing is estimated or rewritten. Breaches added to Have I Been Pwned Careers360: 3,609,421 accounts, added 20 November. Check the breach page Too Lost: 724,323 accounts, added 20 November. Check the breach page If your team's work addresses may be in one of these, check the breach page and the password reuse question, not only the address. How to use a list like this in an hour Start with what faces the internet. VPN and access gateways, firewalls, routers, mail servers and public web platforms are how many ransomware incidents start. Search your inventory by product name, not by memory. "We don't run that" is a claim, and the asset list is the evidence. Patch or apply the vendor mitigation, then confirm the version. A patch that was downloaded but not applied reads as done in a ticket and is still exploitable. If you cannot patch today, reduce exposure: restrict the management interface to known addresses, disable the affected feature, or put the service behind an access gateway you trust. Where this comes from A small collector reads official sources every hour: DNSC, CERT-EU, CERT-FR (ANSSI), CERT-Bund (BSI), the UK NCSC, CISA KEV, Have I Been Pwned and three specialist newsrooms. It copies each item exactly, with its source link. Nothing in this post is written by a model. A security page that paraphrases an advisory wrongly does more harm than no page at all. articles.title: Architecture as Evidence: Reading the Built Environment Through Forensic Investigation
articles.description: Architecture is commonly examined through its visible form, materials and spatial organisation. The physical fabric of a building can also retain evidence of events and alterations that are not apparent from its present appearance. Cracks, repairs and structural changes may indicate when and how a building was modified, while photographs and material fragments can provide further evidence about the circumstances surrounding those changes. Forensic investigation examines these traces, using the built environment and its surrounding records to establish how particular events, alterations or failures occurred.

articles.title: Mumbai Police QR-code ID cards: how to verify an officer and spot impostors
articles.description: Mumbai Police are issuing metal ID cards with a QR code that citizens can scan to check an officer's identity. Here is how the check works, where it falls short, and what to do when someone claiming to be police asks you for money. What happened On Saturday, 21 November 2026, Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis inaugurated a set of technology projects for Mumbai Police. The one most relevant to ordinary citizens is a new identity card for police personnel that anyone can verify with a phone. According to The420 and the Free Press Journal, the new card is metal-based, carries an embossed photograph and a unique QR code, and covers all 51,308 sanctioned posts in the Mumbai Police. The420 and NewsBytes also report an NFC chip, which The420 says authorised staff use to enter restricted police premises. The Maharashtra government sanctioned about Rs 4 crore for the cards in February 2026, both outlets report. A few cards, including some for traffic police, were handed over at the launch. A police official told reporters that printing is complete and every officer should receive a card within a month. The420 adds that carrying the card will be mandatory on official duty, in uniform or plain clothes, including home visits, questioning and investigations. That last detail appears in only one report, so treat it as reported rather than confirmed. The same event launched the Mumbai Police Citizen App, around 50,000 Android tablets for investigators, the Mumbai Police Information System (MPIS) for personnel and administrative records, and an Anti-Narcotics Cell investigation van, as reported by Asianet Newsable (via ANI) and The Live Nagpur. Commissioner Deven Bharti said several of these projects began in 2017, stalled, and were revived in 2022. Today's India Cyber Brief carried this story in one paragraph. This piece looks at the scam the card is meant to counter, what the card can and cannot prove, and what to do when someone claiming to be police contacts you. How verification works As described by The420, FPJ and NewsBytes, the flow is simple: The officer shows the metal ID card. The citizen scans the QR code using the Mumbai Police Citizen App. The app opens an official verification page showing the officer's photo, name, date of joining and current posting. The citizen compares those details with the person standing in front of them. Free Press Journal reports the problem this targets: people posing as plain-clothes officers who approach senior citizens on morning walks and businessmen, sometimes to extort money. When the cards were first approved in May 2025, the Maharashtra Home Department noted that the old printed cards could be copied with basic desktop publishing software, and cited counterfeit IDs used in "digital arrest" frauds. The scam it is meant to stop Police impersonation sits at the centre of two common frauds in India. In-person impersonation A man in plain clothes, sometimes with an accomplice, stops a victim on the street or comes to the door. He flashes a card, claims a "checking" or a pending case, and asks for cash, jewellery or a phone to "hold as evidence". A printed card with a crest and a photo is often enough because few people know what a genuine card looks like. Digital arrest Here the "officer" never appears in person. A call claims the victim's Aadhaar, SIM or a parcel is linked to a crime. The caller moves to a WhatsApp or Skype video call, sometimes from a set made to look like a police station, shows a fake ID card or warrant, and keeps the victim on camera for hours or days while demanding transfers to "verify" funds. Today's brief alone reported a Kolkata case with Rs 1.78 crore lost over 42 days and a Visakhapatnam case of Rs 1.94 crore. The Enforcement Directorate faced the same problem with forged summons. In its press release of 8 October 2025, ED introduced system-generated summons with a QR code and a unique passcode that can be checked on its website, and stated that there is no "digital arrest" or "online arrest" under the PMLA; arrests are made physically under due process. What the card can and cannot prove Analysis: The card is a real improvement for face-to-face encounters. A forger can copy the look of a printed card, but a scan that shows a different face, name or posting exposes the impostor at once. Three limits are worth knowing. A QR code is only as good as the app that reads it. The reports describe verification through the Citizen App. A forger can print a QR code that points to a look-alike website showing whatever photo they choose. If you scan with your phone's general camera, you may not notice. Use the official app, and check that the result opens inside it. A cloned QR shows a real officer, not the person holding it. If a fraudster copies a genuine officer's code, the page will show that officer's real details. The protection is the comparison step: the face on screen must match the face in front of you. The reports do not describe a passcode or one-time check of the kind ED uses for summons. It does nothing for a video call. In a digital arrest, the "card" is held up to a camera. You cannot scan it reliably, and it would not matter if you could. No genuine agency arrests or questions people over a video call or asks them to move money to "verify" it, as ED's release states for its own officers. Analysis: The card helps answer "is this person a Mumbai police officer?" It does not answer "is what this person asking me to do lawful?" Demands for cash, gold, phone handovers or bank transfers are red flags whatever ID is shown. Red flags Situation Red flag On the street or at the door Plain-clothes "officer" refuses a scan, rushes you, or asks you to hand over jewellery, cash or your phone Card shown QR scan opens a web page outside the official app, or the photo, name or posting does not match Phone or video call Claims of an Aadhaar, SIM, parcel or money-laundering case; insistence that you stay on camera and tell no one Documents "Warrant", "arrest memo" or summons sent on WhatsApp; an ED summons with no QR code and passcode Money Any request to transfer funds for "verification", "RBI checking" or bail What to do If you are approached by someone claiming to be police Stay calm and ask to see the ID card. In Mumbai, scan its QR code with the Mumbai Police Citizen App and compare the photo, name and posting with the person. If you cannot scan, or anything does not match, do not hand over anything. Call 112 or the local police station on a number you find yourself, not one the person gives you. Note the time, place, description and any vehicle number, and report it to the nearest police station. If you get a call or video call about an "arrest" or case Hang up. No real officer conducts an arrest or interrogation on a video call. Do not transfer money, share OTPs, install apps or join screen-sharing. Check a summons through the issuing agency's own channel; for ED, use the QR code and passcode or the "Verify Your Summons" option on its website. If you have already paid, call 1930 at once and file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in. Speed matters for freezing funds. Report the number via Sanchar Saathi's Chakshu facility so it can be checked and blocked. If you are an investigator In Mumbai cases, record whether the victim was shown a card, whether it was scanned, and what the scan displayed. A screenshot of a fake verification page is evidence; preserve the URL. If a QR code was used, decode it without opening it (the IGRS QR code checker runs in the browser) and record the destination domain for registrar and hosting requests. Seek call detail records, WhatsApp account details and bank statements through notices under S.94 BNSS, and push 1930 or CFCFRMS reporting early so linked accounts are put on hold. Collect the S.63 BSA certificate for every screenshot, call recording and chat export you rely on. Where the victim describes forged police documents or uniforms, add the impersonation and forgery sections below, not just cheating. Applicable law Provision What it covers Relevance S.204 BNS (IPC 170) Personating a public servant Posing as a police officer, in person or on a call S.205 BNS (IPC 171) Wearing a public servant's garb or token with fraudulent intent Fake uniform, badge or ID card S.336 and S.340 BNS (IPC 465, 471) Forgery; using a forged document as genuine Fake ID cards, warrants, summons S.318 and S.319 BNS (IPC 420, 419) Cheating; cheating by personation Obtaining money by posing as police S.308 BNS (IPC 384) Extortion Money demanded under threat of arrest S.351 BNS (IPC 506) Criminal intimidation Threats during calls or confrontations S.61 BNS (IPC 120B) Criminal conspiracy Call centres, mule suppliers, handlers S.66C and S.66D IT Act, 2000 Identity theft; cheating by personation using a computer resource Video-call impersonation, use of a real officer's identity S.94 BNSS (CrPC 91) Summons to produce documents Records from telecom firms, banks, platforms S.63 BSA (IEA 65B) Certificate for electronic records Screenshots, recordings, chat exports What to watch next Analysis: Three things will decide how much the card helps: whether all personnel actually receive and carry it within the promised month; whether Mumbai Police publicise exactly how a genuine scan looks inside the app, so citizens can spot a fake page; and whether other police forces adopt a similar check. Until then, the old rule still holds: a real officer will not settle a case over a phone call, and will not ask you for money. Scan QR-code IDs to verify Mumbai Police identities (22 Nov 2026) Asianet Newsable / ANI: CM Fadnavis launches new tech initiatives for Mumbai Police (21 Nov 2026) The Live Nagpur: Citizen App, digital IDs, Fadnavis announces technology upgrade for Mumbai Police (21 Nov 2026) NewsBytes: Devendra Fadnavis launches Mumbai Police QR and NFC ID cards (23 Nov 2026) Free Press Journal: Mumbai Police to roll out digital smart ID cards for all personnel (30 May 2025) Enforcement Directorate: Press release on fake summons and QR-code verification (8 Oct 2025) Originally published on IGRS — Intel Grid Research Station. articles.title: I built a tiny programming language for Halloween — then made property tests prove it behaves
articles.description: This post is part of Kiroween 2026 — it's the story of my Skeleton Crew entry, CurseEngine. The idea started with a grumble: every automation tool I rely on asks me to trust rules I can't read. Moderation bots, reminder workflows, digest jobs — the rule fires on real people, and the person accountable for it gets a settings page, not a sentence. So I built the opposite. CurseEngine is a small language where a rule is one line of near-English: curse spam-strikes: when message where count(message by same author flagged) >= 3 within 7 days -> mute author for 1 day; escalate to owner A hand-written parser compiles that to an inspectable graph. A sandboxed executor runs it — no eval, no LLM making the call. And because a rule you can't rehearse is still a gamble, the same executor doubles as a simulator: run it over history and see what would have happened, with zero side effects. Every real action lands in an append-only log — the grimoire — where undo appends a reversal instead of erasing history. One engine, three hosts: GrimMod (chat moderation — a raid bot muted on its third flagged message), Deadbeat (invoice chasing at 7/14/21 days, exactly once per tier), and a standup-digest rule-pack. After the engine's baseline commit, the apps were added with zero changes to the engine package. That diff is the whole Skeleton Crew argument, and it's checkable in the git history. The part I did not expect: the property-based tests found the best bug. The suite runs 1,500 generated event streams through the live executor and the simulator and demands identical outcomes. On the first run it shrank a disagreement about stacked mutes down to a tiny example — a wrong assumption that my hand-written tests shared, which is exactly why they would never have caught it. The generators are wider now (hostile regex patterns, wrong-typed fields, webhook and timer curses), and the parity count is asserted inside the test so it can't silently shrink. The build itself was spec-first in Kiro: four specs, steering files with three inviolables (no exfiltration, the simulator never executes side effects, every action is reversible), and a hook that re-runs the whole property suite every time a curse or fixture is saved — a hook I trust because we deliberately broke a fixture once and watched it fail. Total agent cost: about 50 of the 4,000 hackathon credits. Writing the decisions down turned out to be the cheap part's best friend. Try it live: GrimMod and Deadbeat are both running (links in the repo), and the code is MIT at github.com/pintu544/curseengine. If you run a small community or chase invoices solo, I'd genuinely like to know which curse you'd write first.

articles.title: Practice Mirror: rehearse interview answers, wink for the next question, see which one tightened you up
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge What I Built Practice Mirror is an Android app for rehearsing interview answers alone. Prop the phone up, it shows one question at a time, and you answer out loud. Through the SmartSpectra SDK the front camera does two jobs: Hands-free cards. Wink one eye for the next question, the other eye to go back. No reaching for the phone, so the camera stays still. A question-by-question report. Pulse, breathing, a skin-response (EDA) trace, talking status and expression are tied to the question on screen. Afterwards each question shows its pulse against your resting baseline, and the one that tightened you up most is named. Demo Video link: https://youtube.com/shorts/HE3Zxb83XBo The readings in the video are live, from a friend who agreed to be recorded. Code https://github.com/AbrahamPaulJ/practice-mirror Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, SmartSpectra 3.5.0. Setup steps are in the README. 18 unit tests cover the wink detector and the analysis. How It Responds to Human Signals Face landmarks: per-eye openness. One eye below 60% of its own recent open level while the other stays above 78%, held 350 ms, changes the question. Each eye is compared only with itself, so there is no per-face tuning. Pulse and breathing: live readout, then per question against a 40 second silent warm-up. The SDK's pulse is a 12 second average, so each value is attributed to the question showing 6 seconds earlier. Chest trace: possible breath holds per question. Talking detection and expressions: speaking time and dominant expression per question. No microphone is used. Validation status: plain coaching (too dark, chest not in view). If the chest leaves the picture the SDK stops sending landmarks, so the app restarts it with face metrics only and winks keep working. Tested with a replay harness that feeds video into the SDK: 20 of 20 winks detected, 0 false changes in 90 seconds of normal blinking. Readings taken while speaking are rougher than at rest, and the app says so. Prize Categories Best Thoughtful Real-World Use, and Most Creative or Delightful Use. Consent and Data Handling Consent: the first screen explains what is measured before any camera use. The camera runs only on the warm-up and practice screens, with the preview visible. Nothing runs in the background. Processing: on the phone, inside the SDK. No video, images or audio are stored or sent. Network: only the SDK validating the API key. SDK telemetry is off. Storage: sessions are saved as numbers in the app's private storage until you delete them. Android backup is off. Deletion: per session, or "Delete all my data". Sharing: none. No account, analytics, ads or AI service. Not medical: wellness estimates only, no diagnosis or treatment claim. Agent Session Built with Claude Code (Anthropic), which wrote most of the Kotlin under my direction.
