articles.title: WARN Act and Your ESOP — What Happens to Your Employee Stock Ownership Plan After a Layoff Notice
articles.description: If your employer has an employee stock ownership plan, a layoff notice does more than end your job. It starts a clock on a retirement account that holds your employer's stock — and the rules for when you get paid, how much you keep, and what your shares are worth are nothing like a 401(k). These are reported plans, not confirmed job losses: Layoff Atlas currently tracks 756 WARN notices covering 61,768 reported workers in the last 90 days, led by California (23,980) and Washington (16,420). What an ESOP actually is An ESOP is a tax-qualified retirement plan that invests primarily in your employer's stock. You do not buy in: the company allocates shares to your account each year, usually by a formula tied to your pay, and the shares are held in a trust on your behalf. Unlike a 401(k), your account's value is tied to one company — the one that just laid you off — and you cannot sell the shares like stock in a brokerage account. Vesting decides what you keep Your account may show a balance, but what you can take with you depends on vesting. Federal law sets two minimum schedules, and your plan must be at least as generous as one of them: Three-year cliff vesting: you own nothing until you complete three years of service, then you are 100% vested at once. Six-year graded vesting: you vest 20% after two years, with 20% more each year until 100% after six years. Your own contributions are always 100% vested; the schedules cover company-contributed shares. Leave early and the unvested portion is forfeited. Check one thing right away: the WARN notice period is still employment. Time on the payroll during the 60-day notice window generally counts toward your service — and for someone weeks short of a vesting cliff, those weeks can be worth real money. Confirm your vesting date in writing before your last day. When you actually get paid A layoff is a separation from service, which triggers a distribution. But the timing depends on why you left, and for a layoff the wait can be long. If you retire, become disabled, or die, distributions must begin no later than one year after the close of the plan year in which the event occurred. If you are laid off, the company can wait longer: you must be given the right to start distributions no later than the sixth plan year after the plan year in which you were terminated, and if your balance exceeds the plan's cash-out threshold, you may choose to defer until normal retirement age. Distributions can be paid as a lump sum or in installments over up to five years — your Summary Plan Description says which applies to you. The put option: how private-company shares turn into cash If your employer is publicly traded, distributed shares can be sold on the market. If it is privately held, there is no market — the stock's value is set each year by an independent appraisal — and that is where the put option comes in. When shares are distributed to you, the company must give you a put option: the right to sell the shares back to the company at fair market value. The first window runs 60 days after the distribution. If you do not sell then, the company must offer a second 60-day window starting one year after the distribution date. After that second window, the company has no further obligation to repurchase the shares. The diversification right at 55 Once you turn 55 with at least ten years in the plan, you enter a six-year election period: in the first five years you can move at least 25% of your account into other investments, and 50% in the final year. Each election must be made within 90 days after the plan year closes. If a layoff arrives in your late 50s, check whether this window is already open. Taxes: the rollover decision matters most An ESOP distribution can usually be rolled directly into an IRA or another qualified plan, which defers tax. Taking the cash instead triggers the standard consequences: 20% mandatory federal withholding on the taxable portion, plus a 10% early-withdrawal penalty if you are under 59½, on top of ordinary income tax. With months of no income ahead, cashing out is tempting — but compare the after-tax amount with what a rollover preserves first. What to do this week Get your Summary Plan Description and find the vesting, distribution, and put-option sections. Confirm your vesting percentage and date in writing. Ask for the distribution timing in writing. Mark the put-option windows, and ask for the latest appraisal. Check your diversification election if you are 55 or older with ten years in the plan. Do not elect a cash distribution until you have compared it with a direct rollover to an IRA. A WARN notice gives you 60 days of warning about the job. Give your ESOP the same attention: the vesting, timing, and rollover choices you make in the first weeks are much harder to undo later. Data source: Layoff Atlas

articles.title: Gaming Active Sessions API: Show Users Devices With Bounded Recovery Evidence
articles.description: A gaming account's recovery bill includes the API reads needed to show users active sessions and devices, recovery messages, retained security evidence, and support investigation. Start with the term the design can inflate: copying every inventory response retains a record count proportional to reads multiplied by sessions returned. In an illustrative review workload of 100 page loads returning 6 sessions each, that means 600 session observations. Keeping one outcome per review produces 100 outcome records instead, before any separately required revocation evidence. These are record counts, not measured costs; record sizes, billing terms, and message volume determine which term dominates the actual invoice. Short answer: show users their active sessions from the authoritative per-user inventory, let them revoke an individual session while keeping their current device signed in, and put the option to end everything behind a separate, explicit action. For email-and-password game accounts, make this inventory part of recovery. Bound the evidence you retain separately from the sessions that remain active. Infrai offers one REST API with no SDK required, one key, and one bill for auth and recovery email. Swapping the vendor behind a capability preserves the contract, so the calling code doesn't change. Plain HTTP lets a Node.js account backend and a Python recovery tool use the same interface without installing separate vendor SDKs. The single API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules, reducing credential handoffs when the recovery flow needs both account operations and email. Public discovery also exposes request and response schemas with no key required, letting the backend team inspect the recovery boundary before integration. The trade-off is concentrating service access in one platform. Teams requiring separate identity and mail service boundaries should evaluate Supabase Auth with SendGrid for that split. A fixed request contract doesn't by itself migrate identities, session state, or mail configuration. What does the recovery bill actually retain? The term to change is repeated snapshot retention. The session authority already answers what is active now. Copying its entire response into another durable store on every page refresh creates historical evidence, but that evidence needs its own purpose, access controls, and deletion policy. For a player who lost access to an email account, an old snapshot can also become a misleading answer to a current question. A session shown yesterday may already have been revoked. Keep those jobs distinct. Use the live per-user list for the account screen. Retain a deliberately smaller recovery outcome when the investigation requires it, with application-defined fields such as the action category, an opaque correlation identifier, and the retention deadline. These are proposed audit fields, not a provider response schema. Establish the retention period with the people responsible for incident response and privacy obligations; a convenient database default isn't a policy. The comparison needs a denominator. An outcome record and a session snapshot need not occupy the same number of bytes, and a single review might generate several security events. Count the records first, then measure their size and required lifetime. Otherwise a tidy spreadsheet hides the part that matters: how much evidence remains available when a player disputes a recovery decision. How should an API show users their active sessions and devices? A player signs in with an email address and password, opens account security, and sees the sessions belonging to that authenticated account. The backend must derive the account scope from the authenticated principal. A browser-supplied user identifier is not authorization to inspect another player's sessions. The per-user listing is the authoritative inventory of active sessions; a local recovery log is historical evidence. Offer an individual revoke action next to each eligible entry. Revoking another session should preserve the current device's session, so the player can finish checking the account. Treat the current session deliberately: if the player explicitly ends it, the interface should explain that they will be signed out. Don't label an action as ending another device and then terminate the recovery session as a side effect. Keep the panic control separate. An action labeled "End all sessions" has a different consequence from removing one unfamiliar entry. Make that consequence explicit before execution, and define how the player returns through the sign-in or recovery flow afterward. Refresh the authoritative inventory after a successful revoke. A stale tab shouldn't continue presenting a removed entry as active merely because an earlier response is still in memory. Device descriptions need restraint. A session inventory is not proof of a person's physical device or location. Show descriptive metadata only when the provider actually returns it, label uncertainty honestly, and don't invent a trusted-device designation from a user-agent string. Account recovery should give the player specific actions without turning weak evidence into an accusation. For a Node.js backend, keep the same authorization boundary: resolve the authenticated player, request that player's inventory, and authorize the selected session before revocation. Language choice doesn't change the acceptance condition. Two open tabs, an unfamiliar session, and a deliberate current-session logout should all lead to understandable results. Count the evidence before choosing its lifetime The implementation should fetch the authoritative inventory without automatically archiving it. This Python 3 standard-library example performs that read without assuming undocumented response fields. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the versioned HTTPS API base from your service configuration, INFRAI_API_KEY to the service key, and RECOVERY_USER_ID to a player identifier resolved by an already-authorized backend operation. Keep the base URL in trusted backend configuration, never in a browser-supplied parameter. import json import os import time from datetime import datetime, timezone from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime from urllib.error import HTTPError from urllib.parse import quote, urlsplit from urllib.request import Request, urlopen base = os.environ["INFRAI_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/") key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"] user_id = os.environ["RECOVERY_USER_ID"] if urlsplit(base).scheme != "https" or not base.endswith("/v1"): raise ValueError("Configure the versioned HTTPS API base") if not user_id: raise ValueError("An authorized player identifier is required") def retry_delay(value, attempt): exponential = 2 ** attempt if not value: return exponential try: server_delay = float(value) except ValueError: deadline = parsedate_to_datetime(value) server_delay = (deadline - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds() return max(exponential, server_delay, 0) def load_inventory(): path = "/auth/session/list_for_user/" + quote(user_id, safe="") for attempt in range(4): request = Request( base + path, headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + key}, method="GET", ) with urlopen(request, timeout=20) as response: if response.status != 200: raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected status: {response.status}") return json.load(response) except HTTPError as error: if error.code == 429 and attempt < 3: continue reason = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace") raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {reason}") from error inventory = load_inventory() print("Inventory loaded; render only documented fields for the authorized player.") Under the earlier hypothetical constant daily workload, retaining records for 7 days means 4,200 session observations versus 700 review outcomes. That arithmetic counts one outcome for each load only to isolate the retention choice. A real implementation should distinguish opening the screen from completing a recovery decision, and count any separately retained revocation events. If the same player refreshes five times, five copies of an inventory don't become five independent observations of compromise. The read uses a 4-attempt budget, exponential backoff, and any longer server-requested delay on HTTP 429. Those settings and the 20-second network timeout are example choices. Final HTTP errors include the response body for restricted backend handling; don't forward that body to a public recovery form. The example prints no session payload and performs no writes, so retrying cannot duplicate a revocation. It doesn't implement authorization or render the UI: those remain application responsibilities, checked against the documented response schema. Deleting a local audit row would not end the corresponding login either. Compare the recovery boundary before choosing a provider The selection criterion is the player's recovery path. A credible comparison asks which system supplies the authoritative inventory, how an individual revoke affects the current session, and where notification state lives. Product names alone cannot settle those questions. Candidate Evaluation emphasis Acceptance condition for this game Supabase Auth with SendGrid An explicit split between identity and recovery mail. Demonstrate how the authorized account identity reaches the mail decision, how retries are coordinated, and how notification evidence connects to recovery outcomes. Auth0 Its documented session-management model and the chosen recovery-mail integration. Demonstrate per-user inventory and individual revocation with the game's actual sign-in flow; check which session and token types the operation covers. Clerk Its documented session model and the account experience built around it. Demonstrate current-session behavior, another-session revocation, and the recovery path using the intended account interface. These are distinct integration approaches to evaluate, not a claim that every product exposes identical session semantics. Supabase Auth plus SendGrid is a reasonable candidate when the team wants identity and mail as separate product decisions and accepts responsibility for connecting them. Auth0 deserves evaluation when its session model fits the application's identity boundary. Clerk deserves evaluation when its session and account experience fits the player-facing flow. For each, inspect the documentation and run the same acceptance cases; don't infer that a session operation ends every kind of credential merely from its name. No provider choice removes the delivery question. A successful notification request is not evidence that a recovery message reached the inbox. Keep recipient checks, applicable suppression policy, and delivery evidence in the recovery design. Don't send another recovery message just because the player refreshed the session list. Inventory reads and message retries are different events, and conflating them makes both the bill and the player's inbox harder to explain. The comparison should end with a small demonstration: preserve the current session when removing another one, explicitly sign out when ending the current session, and make the panic action end everything it promises to end. Then inspect the recovery evidence left behind. A polished list of device names isn't enough. Keep enough evidence to explain the decision Retain the minimum recovery evidence that serves a defined investigation and privacy purpose. A correlation identifier can connect the recorded decision to restricted operational evidence without placing the full inventory or message contents into every support record. Define which evidence expires, who may read it, and how its deletion affects an unresolved player dispute. The illustrative 7-day window above is arithmetic, not a recommended compliance deadline. Choose the provider that passes the inventory and revocation checks, then make recovery evidence a deliberate retention decision. Keep recovery-mail delivery evidence only for its defined operational purpose; don't treat an accepted send request as a completed recovery. A player whose email access is lost still needs a separately approved recovery path, rather than an endless stream of new codes. Stop keeping full inventory snapshots on every page refresh and unnecessary copies of recovery-message bodies. That sacrifices some historical reconstruction: after deletion, support may be unable to establish exactly which session descriptions a player saw during an earlier review. Record the decision and the evidence policy clearly enough that this limit is understood before a disputed takeover arrives. Further reading References for the security boundary and the competing session models: OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html Supabase Auth sessions: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/sessions Auth0 session layers: https://auth0.com/docs/manage-users/sessions/session-layers Clerk session management: https://clerk.com/docs/guides/secure/session-options SendGrid email delivery events: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid/for-developers/tracking-events/event

articles.title: Europe SMS Alert API: Property Notices, Sender Registration, and Inbound Evidence
articles.description: Europe SMS Alert API: Property Notices, Sender Registration, and Inbound Evidence Option Pick this when Template ownership decision Evidence to require before rollout Twilio Its documented SMS segmentation rules help you evaluate the approved notice text. Decide who approves wording and who checks the rendered message. A trace from the approved text to a particular send and its subsequent status. Vonage Your team already has an evaluated integration and wants to keep that operational knowledge. Require a named owner for changes made outside the application repository. Verify sender registration, inbound handling, and status retrieval for each destination. Amazon SNS Your existing notification workflow makes it a serious candidate for an acceptance test. Establish where the authoritative template lives before adding another publisher. Test destination coverage, sender requirements, reply handling, and available delivery evidence. Mailgun Email is an approved companion channel and merits a separate evaluation. Retain the approved email revision separately from the SMS revision. Verify domain setup and email evidence; an email evaluation does not qualify an SMS sender. A plain REST service A small alerting workflow can accommodate polling and application-owned compliance checks. Keep approval and template versions under the property manager's control. Correlate each send with the frozen notice and the status observations collected later. TL;DR: For a property manager sending a compliance notice, start with an application-owned template, a frozen message snapshot, and one evaluated SMS transport. Choose the least complex transport that meets your sender-registration and evidence requirements. A startup serving the US and Europe must also evaluate destination rules, GDPR obligations, and inbound handling. A successful API request alone doesn't establish that the tenant received a legally sufficient notice. Keep the text. An audit question is painfully specific: which wording went to which recipient, under whose approval, and what happened afterward? A dashboard's green send counter cannot answer that. The useful comparison axis is template ownership: whether your team can reconstruct the exact notice after someone edits a shared template. This field guide treats the provider comparison as part of that evidence problem, rather than choosing on a headline unit price. Which SMS alert API alternatives fit Europe sender registration and inbound needs? Twilio is worth evaluating when message composition is already a concern. Its SMS character-limit documentation explains segmentation and encoding, a concrete issue when approved wording includes punctuation or characters that alter the message's encoding. Give the legal or operations reviewer the rendered text, then check its encoding and segmentation before approval. Don't infer the final transmitted message from the template's character count alone. Pick Vonage when an existing, evaluated integration gives your team a useful starting point. That is an organizational advantage, not a claim that it wins every destination. Make the evaluation specific: demonstrate the required sender identity, retrieve the evidence your audit process needs, and exercise the intended reply path. If a hosted template is part of the proposed setup, require a way to retain the approved revision in your own record before choosing it. Amazon SNS belongs in the comparison when the startup already organizes notifications around a publishing workflow. Pick it only after the property-notice acceptance test succeeds. In particular, the presence of SMS in a product does not settle how your chosen sender will receive replies or how operations will reconstruct a notice. Those are questions for the tested destination and configuration. Existing infrastructure can shorten adoption, but it doesn't replace that test. Infrai fits simple alerts through one REST API with no SDK required, using a single API key and unified billing across services. Any language that can make an HTTP request can call it. Shared credentials and billing can simplify ownership and reconciliation if an approved email channel joins the SMS workflow. For this workflow, evaluate a polling-based design with application-owned compliance logic. Polling is a trade-off. It is not suitable for a team whose requirement is immediate, conversation-like reply handling. In that case, compare the tested reply workflows of the communications suites before committing. Mailgun belongs in a separate email-channel evaluation if the notice policy permits email; it does not replace the SMS acceptance test. Keep one approved source of wording, but approve the rendered output for each channel separately. These are selection rules, not a measured ranking. The comparison does not establish equivalent country coverage, GDPR compliance, or delivery guarantees across these products. Resolve those questions with the intended destination, sender type, provider agreement, and acceptance-test evidence. The provider references below are starting points for that work. Freeze the approved message before sending it Diagram in words: approved template revision → rendered notice snapshot → durable send intent → transport attempt → provider observations → audit view. That ordering matters. If the application queues only a template identifier and renders it later, an edit between approval and execution can change what gets sent. Store the rendered message before the transport sees it. Retain the template revision, the approval reference, and a stable notice identifier alongside it. The example below uses fictional property data and a short notification that points the tenant toward a secure portal; it is an engineering fixture, not legally approved notice wording. Approval comes first. Here is the narrow implementation worth getting right first. This TypeScript example runs locally without credentials or network access. It freezes one notice, computes a digest over its text and revision, and keeps repeated observations from producing duplicate audit entries. The application-defined fields are internal records, not a vendor request or response schema. import { createHash } from "node:crypto"; type Notice = Readonly<{ noticeId: string; propertyId: string; recipientRef: string; templateRevision: string; approvalRef: string; body: string; contentDigest: string; }>; type Observation = Readonly<{ sourceEventId: string; observedAt: string; providerState: string; const audit: Observation[] = []; const observation: Observation = { sourceEventId: "example-observation-01", noticeId: notice.noticeId, observedAt: "2026-11-19T08:00:00Z", providerState: "example-provider-state", }; appendObservation(observation); The digest identifies the saved content. It doesn't prove approval, delivery, or protection against tampering. The approval reference must resolve to an actual approval record, and the snapshot needs durable storage with appropriate access and retention controls. Likewise, the in-memory array and set demonstrate the record semantics only. A production implementation needs persistent records and an atomic uniqueness constraint, so a process restart or two workers cannot defeat deduplication. Consider the illustrative revision r3: it is approved and queued, then an editor replaces the portal wording in r4 before dispatch. Rendering from the current template would silently send r4 under an r3 approval reference. Rendering from the frozen snapshot preserves the intended wording. The audit record can then explain both the revision that was approved and the content associated with that send intent, without guessing which template happened to be current when a worker ran. Notice the deliberately opaque provider state. An adapter should retain the original observation and map only documented statuses into the application's vocabulary. Don't quietly turn an unknown status into “delivered.” If a source supplies a stable event identifier, use it for deduplication; otherwise, define and test a deterministic observation identity using the documented response fields. An application-generated timestamp on every poll is a poor identity because it makes the same underlying observation look new each time. There are two distinct duplicate problems here. Observation deduplication keeps the audit readable. Send idempotency keeps a transport retry from creating another notice. Persist the send intent before making the request, reuse the same logical identity for that intent's retries, and verify the selected transport's supported idempotency contract. A newly approved notice revision needs an explicit new intent; changing the text under an existing retry identity makes reconciliation ambiguous. Instrument the evidence gap Before: a single “messages sent” chart. After: an operator can follow one notice from approval through dispatch and see when its latest delivery observation was collected. That's a useful teaching example because the second view exposes what the first chart hides. Watch the collector. Keep routine logs small. Record the notice identifier, template revision, request correlation identifier when available, attempt outcome, and observation time. Store the recipient mapping and approved message in the controlled audit store instead of copying tenant details into every log line. The application can join them during an authorized investigation. This improves the usefulness of logs without treating general logging retention as the notice-retention policy. For a polling design, measure observation age separately from send latency. An illustrative 60-second polling interval adds up to roughly one polling interval of observation delay even when retrieval succeeds on schedule; processing, pagination, and upstream reporting can add more. That interval is a design example, not a measured provider guarantee. Alert on an old polling checkpoint as well as unresolved sends, or a stopped collector can leave a reassuring dashboard full of yesterday's results. Replies deserve their own checkpoint. Polling can suit simple STOP or help handling, but it requires a worker, durable progress tracking, and a policy for applying suppression before later sends. Establish an acceptable handling delay with the responsible team. A chat-like support conversation has different timing needs and should get a separate acceptance test. This read-only status collector is the transport-side companion to the local snapshot example. Run it in a TypeScript-capable Node runtime with built-in fetch. Configure INFRAI_API_ORIGIN with the service's HTTPS API origin, INFRAI_API_KEY with a secret supplied by your deployment, and NOTICE_MESSAGE_ID with the identifier retained from a send. It prints the actual JSON response without inventing status fields. The origin is deployment configuration; the path is fixed. This GET does not create another notice. collectStatus().catch((error: unknown) => { process.exitCode = 1; }); The four-attempt limit is an example policy. Persist the next polling checkpoint outside this process, and keep the raw response in the controlled evidence store after applying your retention policy. For send operations, establish idempotency separately; this read-only collector cannot prevent duplicate sends. Sender registration belongs before dispatch, too. Registration and sender listing can help production setup where local rules apply, but they aren't a substitute for checking the destination and message category. Put the allowed-destination policy and any country-level spend controls at the application boundary. Keep those checks visible in the audit record as policy decisions, without storing unnecessary personal data in metrics labels. Limits that change the decision An SMS status is transport evidence. It does not by itself prove that a particular person read a notice or that the chosen channel satisfies a jurisdiction's service requirements. Have the responsible legal and privacy reviewers establish the channel, lawful processing basis, retention period, and evidence requirements before rollout. A US startup serving Europe cannot infer GDPR compliance from an API's availability. That limitation matters. Template ownership also has a cost: application-owned templates require an approval interface or a reviewed change process. Provider-hosted editing may suit an operations team better, provided the workflow preserves the approved revision and final rendered content. Choose the ownership model the team can actually operate. Finally, keep the channel boundary explicit. A polling-based SMS and email design needs application orchestration; mailbox verification flows, SMTP relay requirements, or voice, WhatsApp, and RCS requirements warrant separate product evaluation. Domain verification and email sender guidelines matter if email is added, but neither supplies proof that a property notice was legally served. End the acceptance test with a reconstructed notice record, including unresolved outcomes, rather than a screenshot of a successful send. References The SMS segmentation reference supports the composition discussion. The other provider documentation links identify evaluation starting points; they do not establish equivalent delivery, inbound, or compliance behavior. The email guidance applies only if email joins the workflow. articles.title: The Price You See Isn't the Price You Pay: Coupons, Codes and Membership Pricing in Deal Tracking
articles.description: Every deal site has the same dirty secret: the price on the product page is rarely the price at checkout. A coupon code knocks off 20%. A membership price hides behind a login wall. A "clip the coupon" checkbox sits under the buy button, easy to miss and impossible to scrape. If your price tracker only records the listed price, it is tracking a number nobody pays. At Savlume we learned this the hard way. Our early crawler recorded the headline price, and our deal alerts fired on discounts that did not exist — or missed real ones hiding behind a code. Here is how we think about the problem now. Three prices, one product For any given product on any given day, there are usually three different prices in play: The listed price. What the page shows. This is the number most trackers record, and the least reliable signal of what you will pay. The coupon price. The price after a clipped coupon, a promo code, or a lightning deal. Often 10-40% below the listed price, often time-limited, and often invisible to a crawler that does not execute the page's JavaScript or hold the right session state. The member price. Prime, Walmart+, Target Circle, Costco — the price behind a login. Sometimes it is the only real price, and the public listing is a decoy. A tracker that records only the first number will call a product "back at regular price" when a 30%-off code is sitting right there on the page. Worse, it will call something a deal when the coupon expired yesterday and the listing never updated. Why codes are hard to track Promo codes fail in ways that are specific and annoying: Codes are scoped. A code might apply to one color, one seller, or one bundle — not the listing your crawler checks. Our guide pages carry this explicitly: a code that works on one variant and not another is a different deal, not the same one. Codes stack unpredictably. A 20%-off code plus a clipped $10 coupon plus a Subscribe & Save discount can combine, or the retailer can silently apply only the best one. The final price depends on the order the discounts are applied, which the retailer does not document. Codes die silently. A code that worked this morning returns "not applicable" this afternoon, with no change to the listed price. Unless you re-validate the code on every check, your data goes stale without any signal. Membership prices are per-account. Two shoppers can see two different prices for the same product at the same moment, depending on membership status. There is no single "true" price to record — only a price and the conditions attached to it. What we do instead Our approach is boring on purpose: Record the conditions, not just the number. Every price in our pipeline carries its conditions: which code, which membership, which variant, which expiry. A price without conditions is a rumor. Re-validate codes on every check. A code is only "live" if it validated in the last check. The moment it fails, the deal is marked expired — even if the listed price has not moved. Never present a code price as the listed price. When a guide says a product is "$59.99 with code 4J5ZVXVA", the code is part of the price. A reader who cannot use the code does not get that price, and the guide should say so. Separate what we verified from what we were told. This is why our guides carry two labels: retailer-verified, where we matched the price against the retailer page, and source-reported, where the number comes from coverage or a listing we could not re-check. A code price that we validated is retailer-verified. A code price quoted in a roundup is source-reported. The label is the honest part. The takeaway for builders If you are building price tracking, treat the checkout total as the only price that matters — and treat everything upstream of it as a claim with conditions. Record the code, the membership, the variant, and the time you checked. Expire aggressively. And when you cannot verify a price, say so in the open: a label that says "source-reported" is worth more than a confident number that is wrong. That is also the takeaway for shoppers. The next time a deal looks too good, check the conditions before the price. The coupon box under the buy button is where most "deals" actually live — and where most of them quietly die. Savlume tracks real prices across retailers and labels every one retailer-verified or source-reported. See how we verify: https://savlume.com/

articles.title: Tweet Hunter Alternatives in 2026: A Fair Comparison (and What to Use If You Wanted Hypefury on X)
articles.description: A factual 2026 comparison of Tweet Hunter alternatives for X, with prices taken from each vendor's own site, plus a clear note that Hypefury no longer lists X as a supported platform. People look for a Tweet Hunter alternative for ordinary reasons: the price, the wish to avoid connecting another app to X, or the need for a narrower tool (just scheduling, or just follow-and-cleanup) instead of a full growth suite. This article compares a few options using each product's own public pricing and platform list, checked on 22 November 2026. It is not a sponsored roundup and it does not invent test results, user counts or "X% cheaper in real use." Where a page was only partly readable (Typefully's amounts load in the browser), that limit is stated instead of guessed. One of the options is GrowX, a Chrome extension. I will describe what it does and what it does not do as plainly as the others. The store page is here. First, a necessary note about Hypefury Hypefury is still often mentioned in the same breath as Tweet Hunter, Buffer and Typefully. That grouping is now out of date for X. On 22 November 2026, Hypefury's pricing page lists three plans (Flexible, Creator, Pro) and, in its own FAQ, defines a platform as: Instagram, Facebook, Threads, LinkedIn, TikTok and Bluesky. X (Twitter) is not in that list. So if your question is "what should I use instead of Tweet Hunter on X," Hypefury is not currently a substitute, according to its own site. If your question is "I liked Hypefury-style scheduling and I post on Instagram or LinkedIn," it may still be in play — but that is a different job. Hypefury's published prices that day: Flexible is $6 per month per platform ($60 per year per platform); Creator is $19 per month or $190 billed yearly, with all six platforms included; Pro is $39 per month or $390 billed yearly. Yearly billing is described as 12 months for the price of 10. Every plan starts with a 7-day free trial of Creator, and the FAQ says you do not need a credit card to start the trial. Prices are in US dollars, excluding VAT. The rest of this piece focuses on tools that still address X. Tweet Hunter, as it describes itself Tweet Hunter's pricing page (title still "Plans from $49/mo") listed three paid plans on 22 November 2026, each with a 7-day free trial: Discover — $29 per month, 1 X account. The page describes a large tweet library and custom tweets; the $29 tier is the entry plan. Grow — $49 per month, 5 X accounts, and the page presents this as the plan with the AI writer and CRM. Enterprise — $200 per month (the page also showed $199 struck through), unlimited X accounts, and higher AI limits. Yearly billing was offered with a discount badge on the page. Tweet Hunter is an X-focused, connected-account product: you use it as a web app that works with your X account, with features many people specifically buy it for (a viral-tweet library, CRM-style lists, AI writing on the higher plans, auto-DM features described on the page). If those are the features you need, a cheaper extension that does not offer auto-DMs or a cloud CRM is not a like-for-like replacement. An "alternative" should mean "covers the job I actually hired Tweet Hunter for," not "is a social tool with a lower sticker price." Other X options, with prices from their own pages Buffer — buffer.com/pricing, 22 November 2026. Free forever: up to 3 channels, 10 scheduled posts per channel, 1 user, plus an AI Assistant, insights and API access at the levels listed on that page. Essentials is shown as $5 per month per channel when billed yearly ($60 a year, "save 2 months"), with a 14-day free trial and unlimited scheduled posts. A Team plan is listed at $10 per month per channel on the yearly toggle ($120 a year). The page explains that a channel is one connected social account, and that you only pay for the accounts you connect. Buffer is a multi-network scheduler (Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, TikTok and others, as well as X). It is a strong alternative if scheduling across several networks is the job. It is a weaker match if you wanted Tweet Hunter's X-only growth features. Typefully — typefully.com/pricing, 22 November 2026. The page lists a Free plan (1 social set, 1 user, 10 posts per month, limited media, and it presents advanced scheduling / agents / API / MCP as higher-plan items) plus Creator and Business plans. The dollar amounts for Creator and Business load dynamically in the browser; they were not reliably visible in the static HTML fetched for this article, so they are not quoted here. Check the pricing page on the day you subscribe. Typefully remains an X-capable writing and scheduling tool (the comparison table lists X/Twitter among the platforms). Use it as an alternative if you care about a writing-first composer and multi-network publishing, not if you need follow-and-unfollow tooling. GrowX — growxapp.org/pricing, 22 November 2026. A Chrome extension, not a cloud web app. Free plan forever (Safe and Balanced auto follow, up to 10 scheduled posts waiting, analytics for the latest 30 posts, 7 days of unfollower history, reply targets and a cleanup scan). 30-day Premium trial, no credit card. Premium is $1.99 for 30 days, $14.99 for 365 days, or $59.99 lifetime ($29.99 for the first 100 lifetime buyers). Plans are prepaid and do not auto-renew. Payment is crypto via NOWPayments (ETH and BNB Smart Chain). GrowX runs in your already signed-in x.com session and does not ask for an X password or use OAuth. That is the main architectural difference from Tweet Hunter, Buffer and Typefully, which connect accounts. The matching limits are just as real: Chrome must be running for scheduled posts; it is desktop Chrome 116+ only; it does not publish while your computer is off; and it does not offer Tweet Hunter-style auto-DMs or a cloud CRM. The AI writer is Premium, on-device, and falls back to templates if Chrome's built-in model is unavailable. How to choose without a fake score Match the tool to the job: You want a cloud X growth suite (library, CRM, auto-DMs, AI on a higher plan) and you are comfortable connecting X: Tweet Hunter is the product built for that. An alternative only wins if it offers the same kind of workflow, not merely a lower price. You want to schedule on several networks, including X, from a web app: Buffer (and likely Typefully, once you have confirmed current paid prices on its site) belong in that comparison. Start with Buffer's free plan if three channels and 10 queued posts each are enough to test. You want to stay in Chrome, keep data on your computer, and not grant OAuth: GrowX is built for that. Use the free plan or the 30-day trial before you pay. Do not expect it to replace Tweet Hunter features it does not have. You wanted a Hypefury-like scheduler for X: as of 22 November 2026, Hypefury's own platform list does not include X. Look at Buffer, Typefully or GrowX's scheduler instead, depending on whether you need a cloud multi-network tool or a session-based Chrome extension. Two more cautions. First, "free alternative" should mean a usable free tier, not only a lower paid price. GrowX and Buffer both publish a free plan that stays free; Tweet Hunter's public pricing page that day led with a trial, not a free-forever plan. Second, any tool that follows or unfollows for you should be used inside X's rules, at a human pace. GrowX says no tool can promise zero risk; that is the right tone for this category, including for tools not named here. If a session-based Chrome dashboard is what you were actually looking for, start at growxapp.org or the Chrome Web Store listing. If you need Tweet Hunter's cloud growth features, it is fairer to stay with Tweet Hunter, or to keep looking inside that same product category, than to force a cheaper extension to pretend it is the same app.

articles.title: A six-digit code in the inbox does not mean email verification works
articles.description: An end-to-end test requests an email code, finds six digits in a message, enters them, and sees a green checkmark. It proves that one code can complete one path. It says nothing about whether an expired code still works, a resend leaves two valid codes behind, or the same code can be replayed. That gap matters because email OTP verification is a small state machine. Tests should cover the transitions and the boundaries around them, not just the happy path. Start with a behavior table Before writing selectors, write down what the product promises. A useful minimum looks like this: Situation Expected result Correct, unexpired code Verification succeeds for the address that requested it Incorrect code Verification stays incomplete; a clear error appears Expired code Verification is rejected Code submitted twice The second submission is rejected if codes are single-use Resend requested The newest message arrives; behavior of the older code matches the product's policy Delivery delayed or missing The test fails with a useful timeout, not a fixed sleep or a false pass The last detail in the resend row is a product decision. Some systems invalidate the previous code on resend; others allow both until their individual expiry. Make the contract explicit, then assert that contract. Give every run its own recipient Parallel tests that share an email address can read one another's messages. A unique recipient per test run gives the test a reliable way to isolate delivery. Use a new address for retries too, so a delayed email from a failed attempt cannot be mistaken for the retry's code. Create the inbox before triggering the send. Then wait for a message with the sender or subject you expect. A real wait for a matching message is better than waitForTimeout(5000): a sleep is sometimes too short and otherwise makes every run slower. Here is the delivery portion using Playwright's request client and an InboxRhino inbox fixture. The fixture should provide a ready inbox and delete it after each test. Keep the API key in the test runner's environment or CI secrets. import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test'; test('verifies an address using the code delivered to this run', async ({ page, request, inbox }) => { await page.goto('https://staging.example.com/verify-email'); await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(inbox.address); await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send code' }).click(); expect(response.status()).toBe(200); const { data } = await response.json(); expect(data).toHaveLength(1); expect(data[0].to.toLowerCase()).toBe(inbox.address.toLowerCase()); expect(match, 'message should contain a code in the expected template').not.toBeNull(); await page.getByLabel('Verification code').fill(match![1]); await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Verify' }).click(); await expect(page.getByTestId('verified-email')).toHaveText(inbox.address); }); The subject, sender, message template, page selectors, and fixture are examples; replace them with your application's contract. Avoid extracting the first six digits from any message. It might be a support number, an order ID, or a code from a different notification. Assert the recipient too, and make the UI show which address became verified. Test expiry without relying on the wall clock Waiting around for a production-length expiry makes a slow and flaky test. If the application has an injectable clock or a test-only expiry setting, issue a code, advance time past its expiry, and submit it. Assert that verification is rejected and the account remains unverified. Keep that test seam restricted to the test environment. If the app has no controllable clock, test the expired-code branch at the service boundary with a fixed clock, then keep one shorter end-to-end test to prove the actual email and UI path work together. Treat resend as a separate transition Resend behavior catches subtle defects: the second email never arrives, the interface reports success when sending failed, or an older code remains valid against a policy that says it should be revoked. Use the same inbox for a resend test only when the inbox query can distinguish the messages reliably. Capture message identifiers or a delivery timestamp, request the resend, and wait for the next matching message. Then assert the old and new code behavior according to the documented policy. Do not assume that a later received_at proves which UI action caused the message; a delayed message from the earlier request can arrive later. Check the account state, not just the response text “Code accepted” is a weak final assertion if the verification page can accept a code for the wrong account. Assert the email address displayed as verified, or check persisted account state through a test-only API. For single-use codes, submit the same code again and assert it is rejected. For wrong-code handling, check that the account remains unverified as well as checking the visible error. Keep OTPs and full email bodies out of CI logs. Record safer diagnostics such as the recipient, message ID, test-run ID, and whether the verification state changed. Never put a real user's mailbox or production account into an end-to-end test. The goal is not to test every combination of digits. It is to test the small number of state transitions that define the security and user experience of the flow. Once those expectations are written down, the inbox becomes one step in a precise test, rather than a six-digit string that happens to make the suite green. Disclosure: I build InboxRhino, a receive-only inbox API for email tests. The state-machine checks here apply with any test mailbox your runner can read.

articles.title: How ML Models Are Actually Trained: A Beginner’s Guide to the Frontier
articles.description: TL;DR: You almost never need to pre-train a model. The economical path for small teams and researchers is to take a strong open base model → fine-tune it cheaply (LoRA/QLoRA) on your high-quality data → or skip training entirely and use RAG. Pre-training from scratch is for the few labs with nine-figure budgets. This is a conceptual + strategic guide. It covers: How machine-learning models (especially large language models) are actually trained. How to make training economical. How the Chinese labs (DeepSeek, Kimi/Moonshot, Qwen/Alibaba) train differently from the Western frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic/Claude, Google/Gemini). How all of those differ from agentic tools like Kiro. Where specialized research projects (like NeuroJen) sit on that spectrum. How the Prima Mente Alzheimer's Translation Challenge relates to this ecosystem. Facts about third-party models were verified against public sources (technical reports, model cards, vendor docs) as of October 2026. The field moves fast; treat version-specific numbers as "accurate at time of writing." How ML models are trained (the fundamentals) The LLM training pipeline, stage by stage What training actually costs — and how to make it economical The Chinese labs: DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen The Western frontier labs: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google How they differ — a side-by-side Where Kiro fits (it isn't a model maker) Where specialized projects fit The Prima Mente Alzheimer's Translation Challenge How the challenge relates to this project Glossary 1. How ML models are trained At its core, "training" a model means adjusting millions-to-trillions of numbers (parameters/weights) so the model's predictions get closer to the right answers. The loop is always the same: 1. Forward pass — Feed input in, model produces an output (a prediction). 2. Loss — Compare the prediction to the desired answer; compute an error number ("loss"). Lower = better. 3. Backward pass — "Backpropagation": compute how each weight contributed to the error (the gradient). 4. Update — Nudge each weight slightly in the direction that reduces the loss (an "optimizer" like AdamW does this). 5. Repeat — Millions of times over billions of examples. A few ideas that matter for everything below: Parameters (weights): The model's learned knowledge. "A 7B model" = 7 billion parameters. More parameters ≈ more capacity, but also more compute and memory. Tokens: Text is chopped into tokens (~¾ of a word each). Models are trained on trillions of tokens. "14.8T tokens" means 14.8 trillion. Compute: Measured in GPU-hours or FLOPs. This is the dominant cost. The scaling laws: Empirically, performance improves predictably as you scale model size, data, and compute together. This is why frontier models got huge. But bigger is not automatically better per dollar — which is the whole story of Sections 3–4. 2. The LLM training pipeline Modern large language models are built in phases, each with a different purpose: Phase A — Pre-training (the expensive one) The model reads a vast corpus (web text, books, code — trillions of tokens) and learns to predict the next token. This is self-supervised: no human labels needed, the "answer" is just the next word in the text. This phase creates a base model that has broad knowledge but isn't yet helpful or safe. It consumes ~95%+ of the total training compute. Phase B — Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) / instruction tuning The base model is trained on curated input→output pairs (e.g. "Question → good answer", "Instruction → correct completion"). This teaches it to follow instructions and respond in a useful format. Much cheaper than pre-training — thousands to millions of examples, not trillions of tokens. Phase C — Alignment / preference optimization Make the model helpful, honest, and harmless. Techniques: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback): Humans rank answers; a reward model learns their preferences; the LLM is optimized against it (classically with PPO). DPO (Direct Preference Optimization): A simpler, cheaper alternative to RLHF that skips the separate reward model. Constitutional AI (Anthropic): The model critiques/revises its own answers against a written set of principles ("a constitution"), reducing the human-labeling burden. Phase D — Reasoning training (the 2024–2026 shift) Teach the model to "think" before answering — produce a long chain-of-thought, then the final answer. This is often done with reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards (e.g. math/code problems where correctness is checkable). DeepSeek-R1 and OpenAI's "o" series popularized this. It dramatically improves hard reasoning without making the base model bigger. 3. What training costs Why it's expensive Frontier pre-training needs thousands of top-tier GPUs running for months. A single frontier run can cost tens to hundreds of millions of dollars in compute alone — plus data, salaries, and failed runs. This is why only a handful of organizations pre-train frontier models from scratch. The levers that make training economical Lever What it does Who uses it Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Only activate a subset of the network per token (e.g. 37B of 671B). Huge capacity, fraction of the compute per token. DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, Mixtral Low precision (FP8/INT4) Train/run in 8-bit (or 4-bit) instead of 16/32-bit → less memory, faster math. DeepSeek (FP8 pre-training), most quantized inference Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (LoRA/QLoRA) Freeze the base model; train tiny "adapter" matrices (~0.1–1% of weights). Fine-tune a big model on one GPU. Most open-source fine-tuning, specialized research Quantization Store weights in 4-bit for inference/training → fits bigger models on smaller GPUs. QLoRA, llama.cpp, Unsloth Distillation Train a small "student" model to imitate a big "teacher". Cheap models that punch above their size. DeepSeek-R1-Distill, many small models Better optimizers / stability tricks Converge faster / avoid wasteful failed runs (e.g. Muon, MuonClip). Kimi K2 (MuonClip) Data quality over quantity Clean, de-duplicated, well-curated data trains better per token. Everyone serious about results Retrieval (RAG) instead of training Put knowledge in a searchable store and retrieve it at query time rather than baking it into weights. Near-zero training cost. Most production deployments Free/cheap compute tiers Kaggle (free T4 GPUs 30h/wk), Colab, Modal credits, spot instances. Students, small teams, researchers The single most important beginner lesson You almost never need to pre-train. The economical path is: take a strong open base model → fine-tune it cheaply (LoRA/QLoRA) on your high-quality data → or skip training entirely and use RAG. Pre-training from scratch is for the few labs with nine-figure budgets. Everyone else builds on top. 4. The Chinese labs The defining theme of the Chinese frontier labs is efficiency and openness — achieving near-frontier quality at a fraction of the reported cost, and releasing open weights (you can download and run the model yourself). DeepSeek (DeepSeek-V3 / R1) Architecture: Mixture-of-Experts — 671B total parameters, ~37B active per token. You get the capacity of a huge model at the compute of a ~37B one. Scale & cost: Pre-trained on 14.8 trillion tokens using FP8 (8-bit) training, in ~2.788 million H800 GPU-hours. The widely-cited figure is a ~$5.6M compute cost for the main run — one to two orders of magnitude below typical Western frontier estimates. (Caveat: this is the final run's compute, not total R&D, and the comparison is imperfect — but the efficiency is real.) R1 (reasoning): Trained reasoning ability largely through reinforcement learning (GRPO — Group Relative Policy Optimization). Famously, R1-Zero was trained with RL and no supervised cold-start, showing reasoning can emerge from RL alone; the shipped R1 adds a small SFT cold-start for readability. Openness: Open weights under a permissive (MIT) license; detailed technical reports. This is the opposite of the closed Western approach. Kimi (Moonshot AI — Kimi K2) Architecture: MoE — 1 trillion total parameters, ~32B active; 384 experts, 8 active per token. Training innovation: The MuonClip optimizer — the Muon optimizer plus a "QK-clip" technique to keep training stable at trillion-parameter scale (training instabilities are a major hidden cost; fixing them saves wasted runs). Focus: Agentic tool-use — built to call tools and act, not just chat. Notably, base K2 is not a chain-of-thought reasoning model by default; it's optimized for fast agentic action. Openness: Open weights. Qwen (Alibaba — Qwen3 family) A broad open-weight family: dense models (every parameter active) and MoE variants, across many sizes (small enough for a laptop up to very large). Strong on multilingual, coding, and agentic tasks; widely used as a base for downstream fine-tuning because of the permissive licensing and size range. The common thread MoE for efficiency + low-precision training + open weights + published methods. The strategic bet: openness drives adoption, and efficiency makes frontier-ish capability affordable. 5. The Western frontier labs OpenAI (GPT series) Proprietary, closed weights, API-only. Pioneered the modern RLHF-aligned assistant (InstructGPT → ChatGPT) and the reasoning-model wave (the "o" series). Very large (undisclosed) training budgets; strong product/ecosystem integration. Anthropic (Claude) Proprietary, closed weights, API-only. Known for Constitutional AI (aligning the model against a written set of principles with less human labeling) and a strong safety/reliability emphasis — which is why Claude is a popular default for agentic coding (it holds intent across long, multi-step tasks). Google (Gemini) Proprietary, closed weights, API-only, deeply multimodal (text, images, audio, video) and integrated across Google's products. Backed by Google's own TPU hardware and enormous data/compute. Important nuance: Google also publishes the open-weight Gemma family (including the medical MedGemma that many research projects build on). So "Google" spans both closed frontier (Gemini) and open small models (Gemma). Closed weights, API access, large undisclosed budgets, heavy investment in alignment and safety, and productization. You rent capability through an API rather than owning the model. 6. How they differ Dimension Chinese labs (DeepSeek/Kimi/Qwen) Western frontier (OpenAI/Anthropic/Google) Weights Open — download & self-host Closed — API only (except Google's Gemma) Headline strategy Efficiency + openness Capability + product + safety, kept proprietary Architecture trend Aggressive MoE (sparse) Mix; often undisclosed Training precision FP8 pre-training (DeepSeek) Undisclosed; generally higher precision historically Reported cost Dramatically lower (e.g. DeepSeek ~$5.6M run) Much higher (tens–hundreds of $M), undisclosed Reasoning RL-centric (GRPO; R1-Zero showed RL-only works) RLHF + dedicated reasoning models (o-series) Alignment Lighter / varies Heavy (RLHF, Constitutional AI, red-teaming) You can fine-tune it? Yes (open weights) No (closed) — you can only prompt/call it Transparency Detailed technical reports Limited; cards + marketing The practical upshot for a small team: Open-weight Chinese (and Google Gemma) models are the ones you can actually download, fine-tune, and own. Closed Western models are things you call. 7. Where Kiro fits Kiro is not a model maker — it's an agentic development tool (an IDE and CLI). This is a common point of confusion, so it's worth stating plainly: Kiro does not train its own foundation models. It runs on Amazon Bedrock and gives you access to other people's models: Anthropic's Claude (its historical default), OpenAI's GPT tiers, and open-weight models like DeepSeek and Qwen. Its "Auto" mode is a router: it picks the best available model for a given task based on complexity, latency, and cost. That orchestration — plus spec-driven workflows, tools, and a graph-based state engine — is Kiro's value-add, not the model weights. So on our map: the labs in Sections 4–5 make the models; Kiro orchestrates them. Model makers (train) Orchestrators (route+act) Domain fine-tuners (specialize) OpenAI, Anthropic, Kiro (agentic IDE/CLI on Specialized research (e.g. Google, DeepSeek, → Bedrock; routes to Claude/ → MedGemma + LoRA on Moonshot, Alibaba GPT/DeepSeek/Qwen via "Auto") curated scientific data) 8. Where specialized projects fit Specialized research projects (like NeuroJen) sit deliberately at the economical, specialized end of everything above. Base model: MedGemma-4B (a medical-domain model in Google's open Gemma family) — small, open, and already medically literate. Not pre-trained by us. Method: LoRA supervised fine-tuning via Unsloth, on a single free Kaggle T4 GPU (4-bit quantized). This is Section 3's economical toolkit applied end to end: open base + PEFT + quantization + free compute. The novelty — "answer-withholding" tasks: The training signal hides the field we want the model to predict, so it must reason about the body-to-brain link rather than reformat text. Stage 1 before any training — GraphRAG: Retrieval over a Neo4j knowledge graph, which gives value with zero GPU cost and acts as the baseline the fine-tuned model must beat. Honest evaluation: The fine-tuned model is actually queried and judged by an LLM-judge rubric. In one sentence: Where DeepSeek/OpenAI/etc. spend millions to pre-train general models, specialized projects spend ~$0 to specialize an existing open model for one disease — exactly the right strategy for a small research team. We are a consumer and specializer of the ecosystem, not a frontier trainer. 9. The Prima Mente Challenge Prima Mente is an AI-biology company (London/San Francisco) building epigenomic foundation models — large models trained on how genes are switched on/off across cell types (their model line is called Pleiades). They won the $1M ADDI Alzheimer's Insights AI Prize, connecting them directly to the AD Data Initiative ecosystem. The Alzheimer's Translation Challenge A global, free AI competition to find new therapeutic hypotheses for Alzheimer's, run with the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative (ADDI) and partners (NVIDIA, Hugging Face, Nebius, Prime Intellect, Goodfire, Boltz, and more). The data: A brand-new open-source cellular atlas of ~150 million cells — neurons, astrocytes, and microglia. Released in batches, accessed via AD Workbench and Prima Mente's modelling platform. Two stages: Stage 1 (build & evaluate): Every participant builds AI models on the atlas, assessed on a curated set of evals — general benchmarks, harder tasks such as phenocopy (predicting whether a perturbation reproduces a disease-like cell state), and community-proposed evals. Strongest results are shortlisted. Stage 2 (hypothesize & validate): Shortlisted participants each propose one new therapeutic hypothesis with its anticipated molecular/functional phenotypes. Finalists' hypotheses are tested in Prima Mente's wet lab — closing the loop "from biology to target to function." Timeline (as published): When Milestone October 2026 Registration opens (atlas generation underway) November 2026 Community launches (Q&A, teammates) December 2026 Prizes announced Spring 2027 Competition starts (dataset released; model-building + evals) Summer 2027 Hypothesis validation (finalists' hypotheses tested in the wet lab) Key terms: Free to enter; open to anyone (no biology background required — "set up so ML researchers can take part"); Prima Mente takes no rights to your model or discoveries; you may suggest a gene/compound to test at registration. 10. How the challenge relates to this project This is the strategically important part. Specialized projects and the Prima Mente challenge are complementary layers of the same translational-research stack, and the challenge is a natural proving ground for this thesis. The connection in one picture POPULATION / LITERATURE LAYER CELLULAR / MECHANISM LAYER Specialized Project Prima Mente challenge Mines papers → extracts structured 150M-cell atlas (neurons, astrocytes, "peripheral factor → mechanism → microglia) → model perturbations → central pathology" hypotheses phenocopy / therapeutic hypotheses \ / ▼ ▼ A testable hypothesis from the literature becomes a perturbation to evaluate in cells, and (if shortlisted) in Prima Mente's wet lab. Concrete ways they connect Hypothesis generation vs. validation: The specialized project generates hypotheses about the body-to-brain axis. The challenge is literally a hypothesis-validation engine (Stage 2 → wet lab). A finding like "chronic gut inflammation → gut-brain signalling → microglial activation in the hippocampus" is exactly the kind of specific, testable claim the challenge asks for — and the atlas contains hippocampal microglia to test it against. Shared infrastructure (AD Workbench): The challenge data is served through the AD Workbench — the same ADDI cloud environment researchers are applying to use. Work done for one directly builds capability for the other. Shared ecosystem partner (Hugging Face): Hugging Face is a challenge partner and the standard hub for models/datasets. The tooling overlaps significantly. "Translation" is the shared mission: The challenge is named the Translation Challenge because it moves insights from computation to lab-validated biology — which is precisely the "body-to-brain" aim, one layer up (literature) from Prima Mente's layer (single-cell). The register-a-perturbation hook: At registration you can submit a gene or compound you'd like tested. The structured hypotheses produced by the literature-mining front end are a ready-made source of candidate perturbations to propose — turning output directly into challenge input. Why this matters for the roadmap Participating (or at least aligning with the challenge) gives: A concrete downstream validation path for hypotheses (otherwise they're just text). Access to cellular-level data that complements literature-level data. Free compute and a community (NVIDIA/Nebius/Prime Intellect credits via the challenge). A credible, deadline-driven milestone (Spring 2027) to aim the pipeline at. Bottom line: The literature-mining front end and the cellular-and-wet-lab back end are two halves of the same "from papers to validated targets" pipeline. 11. Glossary Term Plain meaning Parameter / weight One of the many numbers a model learns. More = more capacity + cost. Token A chunk of text (~¾ word) the model reads/produces. Pre-training The big, expensive phase: learn language by predicting the next token on trillions of tokens. SFT Supervised Fine-Tuning: teach a base model to follow instructions with input→output pairs. RLHF Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: align a model to human preferences. DPO Direct Preference Optimization: a simpler, cheaper RLHF alternative. Constitutional AI Anthropic's method: the model self-critiques against written principles. MoE Mixture-of-Experts: activate only a subset of the network per token → big capacity, low per-token compute. LoRA / QLoRA Train tiny adapter weights (optionally on a 4-bit model) instead of the whole model → cheap fine-tuning. Store/run weights in fewer bits (FP8/INT4) → less memory, faster, cheaper. Train a small "student" to imitate a big "teacher". GRPO Group Relative Policy Optimization — the RL method behind DeepSeek-R1's reasoning. MuonClip Kimi K2's optimizer (Muon + QK-clip) for stable trillion-parameter training. RAG / GraphRAG Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetch knowledge at query time instead of baking it into weights (GraphRAG uses a knowledge graph). Open vs closed weights Open = you can download & fine-tune the model; closed = API access only. Base vs instruct model Base = raw pre-trained; instruct = after SFT/alignment, ready to follow instructions. Phenocopy When a perturbation makes a cell look/behave like it has a disease — a key challenge eval.

articles.title: Our Newest Lorries Update Their Own Software Overnight and Nobody in My Department Approves It
articles.description: Of our seventy lorries, the twelve delivered this year are the first that receive software updates from their manufacturer over the mobile network. Software in a modern lorry manages the engine, the gearbox, the braking systems and the driver's displays. Until now it changed only when a lorry went into a workshop, where a technician connected a laptop and a fitter signed the job sheet. A United Nations regulation on vehicle software updates, known as R156 and adopted for new vehicles across Europe, requires manufacturers to manage updates as a controlled process. It covers updates sent over the air, makes sure an update can be installed safely, and requires the driver to be told what it will change. That is reassuring about the manufacturer. It says nothing about us. In September two of the new lorries installed an update overnight in our yard. The next morning the dashboard showed a new warning message, which the release notes described as a change to how tyre pressure readings are displayed. The release notes had been posted to the manufacturer's fleet portal, which nobody in our transport office signed in to. One driver rang in thinking his lorry was faulty and waited forty minutes for an answer. No harm was done. It was simply the first time a supplier had changed the behaviour of our equipment, on our premises, without anyone in the company knowing it was going to happen. For twenty years my department has managed software on things that stay in buildings. Our fleet is becoming a set of computers on wheels, changed by someone else on a schedule they choose. So the transport manager and I have agreed how we will treat them before the rest of the fleet catches up. Each lorry's software version is now recorded in the asset register next to its servicing history. The fleet portal is checked every week, and its notices come to the transport office and to my service desk. Where the manufacturer lets us choose, updates install on Saturday nights, when most of the fleet is parked. Any update that changes what a driver sees or does is briefed to drivers before it installs, in the same way as a change to our handheld software. When software reaches the things that move your goods, change management has to reach them as well, and someone has to decide whose job that is before the first update arrives. – Serguey Shinder
